title: Fresh water and salt water: why so little of Earth's water can be drunk

summary.text: Water covers most of the Earth, yet people in many places run short of water to drink. The reason is salt. Out of every 1,000 parts of Earth's water, about 975 are salty and only 25 are fresh. Of those 25 fresh parts, about 17 are frozen as ice and about 7 and a half lie under the ground. All the fresh lakes and rivers of the world together make less than one tenth of one part. Freezing and evaporation both take water out of salt water and leave the salt behind. That is how the sea keeps making fresh water.
summary.art: A one-litre bottle of water on a kitchen counter, with five teaspoons of water in a small steel katori beside the bottle and one single drop on a dark plate.

intro.hook: From space the Earth looks blue, because water covers most of the surface. So why does a sailor in a lifeboat, with water all around, have nothing to drink?
intro.text: The water around the sailor is sea water, and sea water is salty. A person who drinks sea water ends up with less water in the body than before. In this unit you measure how much of Earth's water is fresh. You freeze salty water to see where the salt goes. You put sticks of potato in salty water to see what salt does to living cells. You melt ice that is already floating in water. You also melt ice that rests above the water, the way ice on land does. Then you see which one raises the level. Then you take water from a jar of fresh and salty layers, as the people of an island do.
intro.art: A small lifeboat with one sailor on a wide blue sea under a hot sun, holding an empty steel tumbler.

outcomes: I can say how fresh water, brackish water and sea water differ, using grams of salt in a litre.
I can share out Earth's water in numbers: salty, ice, groundwater, and lakes and rivers.
I can name the three forms of water, say what changes one into another, and say where each is found on Earth.
I can explain why freezing and evaporation leave salt behind, using evidence from Freeze the Sea.
I can explain why drinking sea water dries out the body, using evidence from the Potato Test.
I can name the main sources of fresh water and what people use them for, and say why fresh water floats on salt water near the sea.
I can say which melting ice raises the sea and which does not, using evidence from Ice on Land, Ice on Sea.
I can plan a fair test, taste without knowing which sample is which, and say what the results show.

terms.meaning: Water with very little salt dissolved in it: less than 1 gram in a litre. Rain, rivers, most lakes, most groundwater and glacier ice are fresh water.
terms.example: The Kaveri carries fresh water. A litre of river water usually holds only a small part of a gram of salts.
terms.art: A clear river running over stones with a steel tumbler being filled from the river.

terms.meaning: The salty water of the seas and oceans. A litre of sea water holds about 35 grams of dissolved salts, mostly common salt.
terms.example: A litre of sea water, dried in the sun, leaves about 6 level teaspoons of salt.
terms.art: A wave breaking on a beach, with a small heap of white salt drawn beside a one-litre bottle.

terms.meaning: Water that is saltier than fresh water but less salty than the sea. It is found where rivers meet the sea.
terms.example: Chilika in Odisha is brackish. Rivers bring fresh water into Chilika and the tide brings sea water in.
terms.art: A wide lagoon with a river entering on one side and a narrow opening to the sea on the other.

terms.meaning: How salty water is. It is measured as grams of dissolved salts in one litre of water.
terms.example: The salinity of sea water is about 35 grams in a litre. The salinity of the Dead Sea is about 340.
terms.art: Three tumblers in a row with a small, a medium and a large heap of salt drawn under them.

terms.meaning: To spread out in a liquid as particles too small to see. A dissolved substance is still there.
terms.example: Salt stirred into water dissolves. The water looks clear but tastes salty.
terms.art: A spoon stirring salt into a tumbler of water, with the grains fading as they sink.

terms.meaning: The three forms, or states, that water takes. Ice is the solid form, water is the liquid form and water vapour is the gas.
terms.example: An ice cube, the water in a tumbler and the invisible vapour above a wet cloth are all water.
terms.art: An ice cube, a tumbler of water and a wet cloth on a line with faint wavy lines rising from the cloth.

terms.meaning: Water in the form of a gas. It is invisible and is mixed into the air everywhere.
terms.example: The drops on the outside of a cold bottle come from water vapour in the room's air.
terms.art: A cold steel bottle on a table with drops forming on the outside.

terms.meaning: To freeze is to change from liquid to solid when heat leaves. To melt is to change from solid to liquid when heat enters. Pure water does both at 0 degrees Celsius.
terms.example: Water in the freezer freezes into ice. Ice on a plate in the room melts into water.
terms.art: An ice tray half filled with water and half with ice cubes, with an arrow pointing each way.

terms.meaning: To evaporate is to change from liquid to gas. To condense is to change from gas back to liquid.
terms.example: Wet clothes dry because their water evaporates. A cold tumbler gets wet because vapour condenses on it.
terms.art: A wet shirt on a line in the sun, and a cold tumbler with drops on the outside.

terms.meaning: A very large, thick body of ice on land, made from snow pressed down over many years. A glacier moves slowly downhill.
terms.example: The Gangotri glacier in Uttarakhand is about 30 kilometres long. The Bhagirathi river begins where the glacier melts.
terms.art: A long tongue of grey-white ice between two rocky mountain sides, with a stream running out from an ice cave at the lower end.

terms.meaning: A layer of glacier ice that covers a whole land. Earth has two: one on Antarctica and one on Greenland.
terms.example: The ice on Antarctica is about 2 kilometres thick on average.
terms.art: A flat white land stretching to the horizon with one small research hut and a flag.

terms.meaning: Ice that forms when the surface of the sea freezes. It is much less salty than the sea water it formed from.
terms.example: In winter the sea around the North Pole is covered with floating sea ice.
terms.art: Flat plates of white ice floating on dark sea water with gaps between them.

terms.meaning: A large piece of ice that has broken off a glacier or an ice sheet and floats in the sea. An iceberg is fresh water.
terms.example: An iceberg floats with about nine tenths of the ice under the water.
terms.art: An iceberg in the sea drawn with a small white top above the water line and a much larger blue part below.

terms.meaning: The height of the surface of the sea. It rises when more water flows into the sea, or when sea water warms and takes up more room.
terms.example: Ice sliding off Antarctica into the sea raises the sea level. Ice that already floats on the sea does not.
terms.art: A harbour wall with a mark on it, and the sea water standing at a line near the top of the mark.

terms.meaning: Water that lies on top of the land: rivers, lakes, ponds and reservoirs.
terms.example: Mumbai's drinking water comes from surface water, held in lakes such as Tansa and Vihar.
terms.art: A lake between low hills with a dam wall and a pipe leading away towards a city.

terms.meaning: Water under the ground. It fills the small gaps between grains of soil, sand and rock.
terms.example: A borewell is a narrow pipe drilled down to groundwater.
terms.art: A cut-away view of the ground with a well, and blue water filling the gaps between grains below a wavy line.

terms.meaning: The movement of water through the thin skin of a living cell, from the less salty side to the more salty side.
terms.example: A stick of potato in very salty water goes limp, because water leaves the potato's cells by osmosis.
terms.art: A stiff potato stick beside a bent, limp potato stick, with small arrows showing water leaving the limp stick.

terms.meaning: The tiny living unit that the bodies of plants, humans and other animals are built from. Each cell is a small bag of watery liquid inside a thin skin.
terms.example: A potato is built of millions of cells. So is your tongue.
terms.art: A magnified view of potato tissue showing many box-shaped cells packed together.

terms.meaning: The wide mouth of a river, where fresh river water meets salt water from the sea.
terms.example: The Hooghly meets the Bay of Bengal in an estuary. The water there is brackish.
terms.art: A river widening as it reaches the sea, with brown river water spreading over blue sea water.

terms.meaning: Taking the salt out of sea water to make fresh water. It needs a lot of energy.
terms.example: A plant at Minjur, near Chennai, makes drinking water from the Bay of Bengal.
terms.art: A long low building beside the sea with large pipes going into the waves and other pipes leading inland.

terms.meaning: A test in which the person who tastes or judges does not know which sample is which. It stops a guess from changing the result.
terms.example: In Freeze the Sea, a grown-up gives you three drops to taste and does not tell you which is which.
terms.art: A child with eyes closed tasting a drop from a spoon held by a grown-up, with three small labelled bowls on the table.

explanations.concept: Fresh water, brackish water and sea water
explanations.definition: Fresh water holds less than 1 gram of dissolved salts in a litre. Sea water holds about 35 grams. Brackish water is in between.
explanations.description: All natural water has something dissolved in it. The amount is what matters. A litre of rain or river water holds a small part of a gram of salts, and you cannot taste them. A litre of sea water holds about 35 grams, which is about 6 level teaspoons. Most of it is common salt, the same salt as in your kitchen. Water between the two is called brackish. Scientists call the saltiness of water its salinity. India's standard for drinking water says half a gram of dissolved salts in a litre, or less, is best. So sea water is about 70 times too salty to drink.
examples: Rain water has almost no salt in it.
The Kaveri at Srirangam is fresh. A litre of its water holds only a small part of a gram of salts.
Chilika lagoon in Odisha is brackish. It is saltier in summer than in the monsoon.
The Arabian Sea holds about 36 grams of salts in a litre.
The Dead Sea, between Jordan and Israel, holds about 340 grams of salts in a litre.
explanations.art: Five tumblers in a row labelled rain, river, lagoon, sea and Dead Sea, with a larger heap of salt drawn under each one.

explanations.concept: How Earth's water is shared out
explanations.definition: Out of every 1,000 parts of Earth's water, about 975 are salty and about 25 are fresh. Most of the fresh water is ice or groundwater.
explanations.description: Water covers about 71 out of every 100 parts of Earth's surface. Scientists have added up all of that water. Out of every 1,000 parts, about 975 are salty. Nearly all of the salty water is in the seas, and a little is salty groundwater and salt lakes. Only 25 parts are fresh. Of those 25, about 17 are frozen in glaciers and ice sheets. About 7 and a half are groundwater. The small amount left is less than half of one part. It holds frozen soil, lakes, rivers, the water in the air and the water in all living beings. All the fresh lakes and rivers together make about 7 hundredths of one part. Yet most cities take their water from lakes and rivers.
examples: In One Litre Earth, a 1 litre bottle stands for all of Earth's water. Of that bottle, the fresh water is only about 5 teaspoons.
About 3 and a half of those 5 teaspoons are ice. About 1 and a half are groundwater.
All the fresh lakes and rivers together are only about one drop.
Lake Baikal in Russia alone holds about a fifth of the fresh water in all the world's lakes and rivers.
explanations.art: A one-litre bottle beside three small katoris labelled ice, groundwater, and lakes and rivers, holding three and a half teaspoons, one and a half teaspoons and one drop.

explanations.concept: The three forms of water, and where each is found
explanations.definition: Water is found on Earth as a solid (ice), a liquid (water) and a gas (water vapour). Most of Earth's water is liquid.
explanations.description: Ice, liquid water and water vapour are the same substance in three forms. Scientists call these forms states. About 98 out of every 100 parts of Earth's water are liquid, in the sea and under the ground. Nearly 2 parts are ice, in glaciers, ice sheets and sea ice. Water vapour is only about 1 part in 100,000. It is mixed into the air everywhere, and it is invisible. If all the vapour in the air fell as rain at once, it would cover the Earth about 2 and a half centimetres deep. That small amount matters a great deal, because all rain and snow form from it.
examples: Solid water is in the Siachen glacier, the ice on Antarctica, hail and the frost in a freezer.
Liquid water is found in the Indian Ocean, in the Godavari, in a well and inside a coconut.
Water as a gas is in the air above wet clothes and in the air you breathe out.
A cloud is tiny drops of liquid water or tiny bits of ice. A cloud is water that has condensed from vapour.
explanations.art: A mountain glacier, a river flowing from the glacier to the sea, and faint wavy lines rising from the sea into clear air.

explanations.concept: What changes water from one form to another
explanations.definition: Heat entering or leaving changes water's form. Ice melts and water evaporates when heat enters. Vapour condenses and water freezes when heat leaves.
explanations.description: Pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, and ice melts at the same temperature. Water evaporates at any temperature, and faster when it is warm. Vapour condenses when it touches something cool. None of these changes makes new water or destroys water. In One Bottle, Three Forms, the water freezes and then melts. It comes back to the line you marked at the start. One thing does change. When water freezes, it takes up about one tenth more room. So a cupful of ice weighs less than a cupful of water, and that is why ice floats. A lake in Ladakh freezes from the top, and fish live in the liquid water below the ice. Water pipes in cold hill towns can burst in winter, because the freezing water pushes the pipe apart.
examples: An ice cube on a plate melts into a puddle. That is melting.
Water in a tray turns into ice in the freezer. That is freezing.
A wet floor dries because its water goes into the air. That is evaporating.
Drops form on a cold bottle taken from the fridge. Water vapour in the air turns back into liquid on it. That is condensing.
explanations.art: A plastic bottle of ice with the ice standing above a band that marks where the water level was.

explanations.concept: Why freezing and evaporation leave the salt behind
explanations.definition: When water freezes or evaporates, water particles leave the salty liquid. Almost all the salt particles stay in the liquid.
explanations.description: Water is made of tiny particles called molecules. In ice, the water molecules are locked in a regular pattern. A salt particle does not fit that pattern. So as ice grows, the salt stays in the liquid that is left, and that liquid gets saltier. This is what you taste in Freeze the Sea. The ice is not perfectly fresh. Small pockets of very salty liquid get trapped between the ice crystals. Saltier water also freezes at a lower temperature. Sea water starts to freeze at about minus 2 degrees Celsius. Evaporation sorts water from salt even better. Only water molecules fly off into the air. So rain is fresh, although most of it rose from the salty sea.
examples: In Freeze the Sea, the melted ice tastes less salty than the liquid left in the bowl.
New sea ice holds less salt than the sea water under it. The rest sits in tiny pockets of salty liquid.
Sea ice that has lasted several summers is nearly fresh, because the salty pockets drain out.
Salt pans at Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu use evaporation. The water leaves and the salt stays.
explanations.art: A magnified view of ice growing into salty water, with water molecules in a neat six-sided pattern and salt particles pushed into the liquid.

explanations.concept: Ice on Earth: glaciers, ice sheets, icebergs and sea ice
explanations.definition: Glaciers, ice sheets and icebergs are made from snow, so they are fresh water. Sea ice is frozen sea water and holds a little salt.
explanations.description: About 17 of Earth's 25 fresh parts are ice. Nearly all of that ice lies on land. It began as snow. Each year's snow pressed down on the snow below, until it became hard ice. An ice sheet covers a whole land. About nine tenths of the world's ice is on Antarctica, where the ice is about 2 kilometres thick on average. A glacier is a river of ice in a mountain valley. The Himalayas hold thousands of glaciers. In summer their melt water feeds rivers such as the Ganga, the Indus and the Brahmaputra. An iceberg is a piece of glacier ice that has broken off into the sea. Sea ice is different. It forms when the sea's own surface freezes. This difference matters for the sea level. Ice on land adds water to the sea when it slides in and melts. Ice that already floats does not, as you see in Ice on Land, Ice on Sea. Warm sea water also takes up a little more room, and this adds to the rise.
examples: The Gangotri glacier is about 30 kilometres long. The Bhagirathi river flows out of an ice cave called Gaumukh.
The Siachen glacier in the Karakoram is more than 70 kilometres long.
If all the ice on Antarctica melted, the sea would rise by about 58 metres.
Aditi Pant, an ocean scientist, and Sudipta Sengupta, a geologist, are credited as the first Indian women to reach Antarctica, in 1983 and 1984.
In Ice on Land, Ice on Sea, the water level rose when ice above the water melted into it. The level stayed the same when ice that was already floating melted.
explanations.art: A glacier ending in an ice cave with a stream flowing out, and two small figures in warm clothes looking at the cave from a safe distance.

explanations.concept: Groundwater: the largest store of liquid fresh water
explanations.definition: Groundwater fills the gaps between grains of soil, sand and rock. It holds about 100 times as much fresh water as all the lakes and rivers.
explanations.description: Rain soaks into the ground and trickles down until it reaches rock that it cannot pass. There the water fills the gaps between the grains. Wells and borewells take water from this store. In One Litre Earth, groundwater is 1 and a half teaspoons, and all the lakes and rivers are one drop. So most of the liquid fresh water on Earth is out of sight. More than half of India's farm water and most village drinking water come from groundwater. Groundwater moves slowly. Some of it fell as rain last year. Some has been under the ground for thousands of years. Not all groundwater is fresh. Under parts of the Thar desert and near some coasts, groundwater is brackish or salty.
examples: A borewell in Bengaluru may go down 300 metres or more to reach water.
In a mine in Canada, a team that included the scientist Barbara Sherwood Lollar found water that had been shut in rock for more than a billion years.
Water pumped from deep wells in the Thar desert is often too salty to drink.
explanations.art: A cut-away view of land showing rain soaking down through soil into a layer of wet sand, with a borewell pipe reaching into that layer.

explanations.concept: Rivers and lakes, and why some lakes are salty
explanations.definition: Rivers and most lakes hold fresh water, because water keeps flowing through them. A lake with no river flowing out becomes salty.
explanations.description: Rivers and lakes are the smallest store, and the one people use most, because their water is easy to reach. A river carries a very small amount of dissolved salts, taken from rock and soil. In most lakes, a river flows in and a river flows out, so the salts are carried on to the sea. Some lakes have no way out. Water leaves them only by evaporation, and evaporation leaves the salts behind. Year after year the salts build up. Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan is such a lake, and people make salt from it. The sea is salty for the same reason. Rivers have carried salts into the sea for hundreds of millions of years, and only the water leaves.
examples: Wular Lake in Kashmir is fresh. The Jhelum river flows in at one side and out at the other.
Loktak Lake in Manipur is fresh, with floating mats of plants called phumdis.
Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan has no river flowing out, and is salty.
Lonar Lake in Maharashtra fills a crater made by a meteorite. The lake has no outlet, and the water is salty.
explanations.art: Two lakes side by side: one with a river flowing in and out, and one with a river flowing in only, with a white crust of salt on the shore.

explanations.concept: Why we cannot drink sea water
explanations.definition: Sea water is saltier than the liquid inside our cells. By osmosis, the salt draws water out of the cells, and the kidneys use up more water to remove it.
explanations.description: Your body is built of cells, and each cell is a small bag of watery liquid in a thin skin. The liquid in your cells and blood holds about 9 grams of salt in a litre. Water passes through a cell's skin easily, and salt passes with difficulty. Water moves through the skin from the less salty side to the more salty side. This movement is called osmosis. In the Potato Test, potato sticks in very salty water lose water and go limp. Sea water holds about 35 grams of salt in a litre. If a person drinks sea water, the blood becomes saltier, and water leaves the cells. The kidneys must remove the extra salt in urine. But human urine cannot become as salty as sea water. So to remove the salt from one litre of sea water, the kidneys use more water than the person drank. The person ends up thirstier than before.
examples: In the Potato Test, the stick in plain water stays stiff and the stick in very salty water bends.
Salt sprinkled on cut cucumber draws water out, and a puddle forms on the plate.
Sailors in lifeboats are told never to drink sea water.
explanations.art: A person's outline with a tumbler of sea water going in, and a larger amount of water shown leaving through the kidneys.

explanations.concept: Animals and plants who can drink the sea
explanations.definition: Some animals and plants have body parts that remove salt, so they can live on sea water.
explanations.description: Humans cannot live on sea water, but many other beings can. An albatross can spend months at sea and drink only sea water. She has a salt gland above each eye. The gland takes salt out of her blood and makes a liquid saltier than the sea. The liquid drips from the tip of her beak. Sea turtles have salt glands near their eyes, so a sea turtle on a beach seems to cry. Sea fish drink sea water and push the salt out through their gills. Mangrove trees grow with their roots in brackish water. Some mangroves keep most of the salt out at the root. Others let the salt in and push it out through their leaves, where it dries as white crystals.
examples: Gulls, albatrosses and penguins have salt glands.
An olive ridley turtle nesting at Gahirmatha in Odisha sheds salty tears.
Grey mangrove leaves at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu have white salt crystals on them after a sunny day.
A camel can drink water that is a little salty. A person would find that water too salty to drink.
explanations.art: An albatross gliding low over waves with a drop falling from the tip of her beak, and a mangrove leaf with tiny white crystals on the surface.

explanations.concept: Where fresh water meets salt water
explanations.definition: Fresh water is lighter than salt water, so fresh water floats on top where the two meet. Stirring or hard pumping mixes them.
explanations.description: A litre of fresh water has a mass of 1,000 grams. A litre of sea water has a mass of about 1,025 grams, because of the salt. So fresh water floats on sea water, as you see in The Island Well. Where a river enters the sea, the river water spreads over the sea water. Under a small coral island, the rain that soaks into the sand floats on the sea water below. A floating layer of fresh water is a little like an iceberg, because most of it lies below the sea level. About 40 parts in every 41 are under the sea level. So a layer that rises 1 metre above the sea can reach about 40 metres below it. Real layers are thinner, because tides and pumping mix them. People on the islands of Lakshadweep take this floating rain water from shallow wells. Along a coast, fresh groundwater pushes towards the sea and holds the sea water back. If people pump too much fresh water out, sea water creeps inland under the ground. Wells near the shore then turn salty. This has happened along parts of the coast near Chennai.
examples: In The Island Well, clear fresh water stays as a layer above blue salty water until it is stirred.
A well on Agatti island rises and falls a little with the tide, because the fresh water floats on the sea.
At Minjur, north of Chennai, groundwater has turned salty up to about 16 kilometres from the shore.
explanations.art: A cut-away view of a small coral island with a thin layer of fresh water floating on sea water under the sand, and a shallow well reaching the fresh layer.

explanations.concept: What people use fresh water for
explanations.definition: Worldwide, about 7 in every 10 litres of fresh water that people take go to farms, about 2 to industry and about 1 to homes.
explanations.description: People take fresh water from rivers, lakes and groundwater. Most of it grows food. A farm field needs far more water than a family drinks, because a growing plant takes up water all day and gives most of it back to the air. Industry uses water to cool machines, wash and make things such as paper, cloth and steel. Homes use the smallest share. A person needs only 2 to 3 litres a day to drink. India's planners work with about 135 litres a person each day in cities with sewers, for drinking, cooking, washing and the toilet. India pumps more groundwater than any other country, mostly for farms. The same water can be used more than once. Water that cools a machine or washes rice can often water a plant.
examples: Rice paddies in the Kaveri delta are flooded with river water for much of the season.
A cloth mill in Tiruppur uses water in dyeing and washing cloth.
A family in a flat fills the overhead tank each morning for cooking, washing and the toilet.
explanations.art: Three taps drawn side by side, one over a green field, one over a factory and one over a house, with the biggest stream going to the field.

explanations.concept: Should cities make their drinking water from the sea?
explanations.definition: Desalination is the removal of salt from sea water. It works, and people disagree about how much cities should depend on it.
explanations.description: A desalination plant pushes sea water at very high pressure against sheets with holes so fine that water passes and most salt does not. Chennai's first large plant opened at Minjur in 2010. It makes about 100 million litres of drinking water a day. At Kavaratti in Lakshadweep, a plant has made fresh water from the sea since 2005. Desalination gives water even when the rains fail. But it uses a lot of electricity, and it sends very salty waste water back into the sea.
examples: Chennai has plants at Minjur and Nemmeli.
Saudi Arabia and Israel get a large share of their drinking water from the sea.
A lifeboat's hand pump can make a little fresh water from sea water.

perspectives.who: An engineer at a city water board
perspectives.explanation: The sea does not run dry. When the monsoon fails and the lakes are empty, a sea-water plant still gives water every day.

perspectives.who: A woman who fishes near the plant
perspectives.explanation: The waste water is much saltier than the sea. Near the pipe, the fish and the prawns have gone, and my catch is smaller.
Saving rain, cleaning used water and mending leaking pipes cost far less energy for each litre. A city should do these first, and use the sea last.

explanations.art: A desalination plant on a coast with a pipe bringing sea water in, a pipe taking fresh water to a city and a pipe returning salty waste to the sea.

explanations.concept: Is there water deep inside the Earth?
explanations.description: All the numbers in this unit count the water at Earth's surface: the sea, the ice, the groundwater and the air. There may be more, far below. In 2014, the scientist Graham Pearson and his team studied a small diamond from Brazil. Inside the diamond was a speck of a mineral called ringwoodite, which forms hundreds of kilometres down. The speck held water, locked inside the mineral. This water is not a liquid and nobody could drink it. If much of the deep rock is like that speck, the rock could hold as much water as all the oceans. One speck is very little evidence, so this is still an idea.
examples: A mineral can hold water locked inside its own structure and still look dry, as plaster does.
Volcanoes give off steam, so some water does come up from deep rock.
explanations.art: A cut-away view of the Earth with the thin blue ocean at the surface and a band of rock deep below marked with a question mark.

agreed.text: About 975 of every 1,000 parts of Earth's water are salty, and about 25 are fresh.
agreed.evidence: Scientists measured the depth of the seas with echo sounders and satellites, and the thickness of the ice with radar. The Russian scientist Igor Shiklomanov added up the stores in 1993, and later counts agree closely.

agreed.text: Most of Earth's fresh water is frozen, and most of the rest is under the ground.
agreed.evidence: Radar from aircraft shows ice about 2 kilometres thick over Antarctica. Wells, borewells and satellite measurements show how much water the ground holds.

agreed.text: When salt water freezes, the ice holds much less salt than the water it came from.
agreed.evidence: In 1776 Edward Nairne froze sea water in London and melted the ice. The water had no taste of salt. Scientists who drill into sea ice measure the same thing today.

agreed.text: Water moves through the skin of a living cell towards the saltier side.
agreed.evidence: Pieces of potato, beetroot and many other tissues lose mass in salty water and gain mass in plain water. Anyone can repeat this with a kitchen scale.

agreed.text: Drinking sea water makes a person lose more water than they drank.
agreed.evidence: Human urine cannot become as salty as sea water, which holds about 35 grams in a litre. Records of shipwrecks show that people who drank sea water died sooner than those who did not.

agreed.text: Fresh water floats on salt water, because a litre of fresh water has less mass.
agreed.evidence: A litre of sea water has a mass of about 1,025 grams, against 1,000 grams for fresh water. Wells on coral islands hold fresh water that rises and falls with the tide.

challenging.claim: The Earth has so much water that people can never run short.
challenging.for: Water covers about 71 out of every 100 parts of the surface, and the water cycle never stops.
challenging.against: Only 25 of every 1,000 parts are fresh, and most of that is ice. People in a place can use only the rain, river water and groundwater that reach that place.
challenging.context: This is a common belief about water, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: Sea water cannot freeze, so all the ice at sea must come from rivers.
challenging.for: Ice taken from the sea melted into fresh water. Sea water also stays liquid when ponds on land have frozen.
challenging.against: Edward Nairne froze sea water in 1776. It froze at a slightly lower temperature than fresh water, and the melted ice had no taste of salt.
challenging.context: This is an idea that many learned people held about 250 years ago. A simple test showed it was wrong.

challenging.claim: Deeper wells always give better water.
challenging.for: A deeper well reaches water when a shallow well has dried up, and deep water usually carries fewer germs.
challenging.against: Near the sea and on islands, salt water lies under the fresh water. In some places, deep groundwater also holds more dissolved salts, fluoride or arsenic.
challenging.context: This is a belief many people hold when a well is dug. In some places it is true and in others it is not.

challenging.claim: Icebergs could be towed to dry countries to give them drinking water.
challenging.for: An iceberg is fresh water, and one large iceberg holds a very great amount of fresh water. Icebergs melt into the sea unused.
challenging.against: A towed iceberg melts on the way through warm seas, and the towing would cost a great deal of fuel. Nobody has yet done it.
challenging.context: This is a plan that a few engineers have put forward. Most water scientists doubt that it can work.

challenging.claim: When the ice at the North Pole melts, the sea will rise a great deal.
challenging.who: A common belief, repeated in many news stories.
challenging.for: The Arctic ice is melting fast, and the sea is rising.
challenging.against: The ice at the North Pole is sea ice. It already floats, so melting it hardly changes the sea level. The sea rises because of ice on land, such as Greenland, and because warm water takes up more room.
challenging.context: This is a common belief about melting ice. Ice on Land, Ice on Sea tests the idea with a tub of water.

challenging.claim: Desalination will end the world's shortage of drinking water.
challenging.for: The sea holds far more water than people could ever use, and the cost of taking out the salt has fallen.
challenging.against: It still needs much more energy than cleaning river water. Towns far from the sea or high above it would also have to pump the water a long way. The salty waste harms life near the outlet.
challenging.context: This is a claim made about plants that take the salt out of sea water. Scientists and engineers argue about it.

big_questions.q: An albatross drinks sea water and stays healthy. Is 'drinking water' a kind of water, or does it depend on who is drinking?
big_questions.hint: Think about the albatross's salt glands and your own kidneys. What would each of you call fresh enough?

big_questions.q: In Freeze the Sea, the ice and the leftover liquid came from one bowl. Were they ever two different waters?
big_questions.hint: The water particles in the ice and in the liquid are the same kind. Only the salt is shared out differently.

big_questions.q: The rain that fills a river rose from the sea, and the river carries it back. Is the water in a river really fresh water, or is it sea water on its way home?
big_questions.hint: Follow one drop from the Bay of Bengal to a cloud, to the Kaveri, and back.

big_questions.q: Most fresh water is ice far from where people live. Does anyone own the ice on Antarctica? Should anyone?
big_questions.hint: By a treaty of 1959, no country owns Antarctica, and it is kept for science and peace.

big_questions.q: Groundwater under a village took thousands of years to collect. Is it fair for one farm to pump as much as it likes?
big_questions.hint: Think of the people nearby, the people not yet born, and the trees whose roots reach that water.

big_questions.q: Humans use most of the reachable fresh water. How much should be left in rivers for fish, otters, trees and everyone else who lives by fresh water?
big_questions.hint: A river that is pumped dry before the sea has no estuary, and the fish who breed there have nowhere to go.

story.title: The Well That Moved with the Tide
story.note: Ayesha, Ummumma, Yusuf, Hamza and Zubaida are made up. These facts are real: Agatti is a narrow coral island in Lakshadweep, about 7 kilometres long and under a kilometre across. On such islands, rain water soaks into the sand and floats as a thin layer on the sea water below. The water in island wells rises and falls with the tide. Wells that are dug too deep or pumped too hard turn salty. The monsoon reaches Lakshadweep around the start of June. Ummumma is a word for grandmother used by many Muslim families in Kerala and Lakshadweep.
text: Ayesha was ten, and she drew the water for her grandmother every evening.

The well stood behind their house on Agatti. The island was so narrow that she could hear the lagoon on one side and the open sea on the other. It was not a deep well. The rope had seven knots, one for each arm's length, and the bucket touched water near the fourth knot. Ummumma called the water sweet. On Agatti, sweet water meant water with no salt in it.
That year their neighbour Hamza built a new house and dug a new well. He dug far down past the wet sand. He lined the well with nine rings of cement and set an electric pump on top.
"Deep water is clean water," he told everyone.
For a month his tank filled in ten minutes. His wife Zubaida watered a whole row of banana plants with a hose.
Then, in April, Zubaida came to Ummumma's door with an empty pot. "Our water has turned," she said. "The tea tastes of the sea."
Hamza was sure of the reason. "The well is not deep enough yet," he said. "The sweet water must be further down. After Friday I will dig three more rings."

Ayesha heard this while she drew the evening water. As she listened, she looked at the rope in her hands. The bucket had touched water just below the fourth knot. That morning it had touched water just above the knot. She had seen this many times and had never thought about it.

She tied a strip of red cloth to the rope at the place where it met the water. Next morning, before school, she let the bucket down again. The red cloth hung dry, a hand's width above the water. In the evening the water was back at the cloth.

For four days she kept a page in her maths notebook. She wrote the height of the water in the well, morning and evening. After school she walked to the jetty, where the boatmen had painted lines on a post to read the tide, and she wrote that down too. When the tide was high at the jetty, the well was high about an hour later. When the tide was low, the well was low.
"The well goes up and down with the sea," she told Ummumma.
"It always has," said Ummumma. "My mother knew it. Draw at high tide, and the bucket has less far to go."
"But then the sea is under our well. So why is our water not salty?"
Ummumma had no answer. She had never needed one.

Ayesha found the answer on Sunday, and she found it by accident. Her little brother Yusuf kept a hermit crab in a glass jar of sea water for a day, before he put her back on the beach. That morning it rained hard for an hour, the first rain since December. The jar stood under the edge of the roof. Rain ran off the dusty tiles, brown as weak tea, and trickled down the inside of the jar.

When Ayesha picked up the jar, there were two waters in it. At the bottom was clear sea water, where the crab sat. On top lay a brown layer as thick as her finger. That was the rain from the roof. The line between the two was as straight as a line drawn with a ruler.
She tilted the jar. The brown layer tilted too, and stayed on top.

Then Yusuf took the jar and shook it to wake the crab. The crab did not like it, and Yusuf said sorry to her. The whole jar went pale brown. They waited a long time. The two waters did not come apart again.

Ayesha sat on the step and thought about the rope, the tide and the jar. Then she filled a second jar with sea water. She let tea-coloured water run slowly down the inside until there was a brown layer on top, and she carried the jar to Hamza's yard. He was mixing cement for the new rings.
"Hamza uncle, please don't dig," she said.

She showed him the notebook first. "The wells rise and fall with the tide. So the sea is under the whole island, under the sand." Then she held up the jar. "Rain is lighter than sea water. It soaks into the sand and floats on the sea, the way this brown water floats. Ummumma's bucket takes a little from the top. Your well goes down close to the line. Your pump pulls hard, and it pulls the sea up from below. It does what Yusuf did when he shook the jar."
Hamza looked at the jar for some time. "So if I dig three more rings..."
"You will have a well of sea water."
He said nothing. He had paid for nine rings of cement, and he was not a man who liked being wrong. Behind him, Zubaida said, "Try what the child says. It costs nothing to stop digging."

Hamza did not dig. He filled the bottom of his well with coral stones and sand, until it was no deeper than Ummumma's. He lifted the pump's pipe so that it hung just under the surface. He ran the pump for ten minutes in the morning and ten in the evening, and no more. The banana plants got the washing water.
For two weeks the tea still tasted of the sea. Then the monsoon reached Agatti, and it rained for nine days.
On the tenth day Zubaida came to the door with a full tumbler. Ummumma tasted it and passed it to Ayesha.
It was sweet.
Ayesha went on keeping her page of marks long after anyone needed it. She liked knowing what she was doing each time the bucket came up. She was lifting rain off the top of the sea.
story.epiphany: For the parent: on a small coral island, rain soaks into the sand and floats on the heavier sea water underneath. Ayesha's two clues are the well rising with the tide, which shows that the sea is under the island, and the brown rain floating in the jar. A shallow well and a bucket take only the top of the fresh layer. A deep well and a strong pump draw the salt water up, and once the two are mixed they do not separate by themselves. Only new rain rebuilds the fresh layer.
ask: The well rose and fell with the tide. What did that tell Ayesha about what lies under the island?
Why did the brown rain water stay on top of the sea water in the jar?
Hamza thought a deeper well would reach sweeter water. Why was a deeper well the wrong answer on this island?
After Hamza changed his well, the water stayed salty for two weeks. What had to happen before it turned sweet?

games.title: Fresh, Salty or In Between? A card sort
games.context: This is a card game about real waters of India and the world. Each card names one water. You decide if it is fresh, salty or in between, and say why. The answer is on the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided water cards (the answer is on the back)

items.f: The Bay of Bengal
items.b: SALTY. This is sea water, with about 33 grams of salt in a litre. Big rivers make the bay a little less salty than the open ocean.

items.f: The Arabian Sea
items.b: SALTY. About 36 grams of salt in a litre. Few rivers flow in and a lot of water evaporates, so this sea is a little saltier than the Bay of Bengal.

items.f: Wular Lake, Kashmir
items.b: FRESH. The Jhelum river flows in at one side and out at the other, and carries the salts onward.

items.f: Sambhar Lake, Rajasthan
items.b: SALTY. No river flows out. Water leaves only by evaporation, and the salt stays. People make salt here.

items.f: Chilika, Odisha
items.b: IN BETWEEN. Chilika is a lagoon. Rivers bring fresh water in and the tide brings sea water in, so the water is brackish.

items.f: Loktak Lake, Manipur
items.b: FRESH. Rivers flow in and out. Mats of plants called phumdis float on this lake.

items.f: The Vembanad backwaters, Kerala
items.b: IN BETWEEN. The backwaters join the sea, so they are brackish. A barrier at Thanneermukkom keeps one part fresher for rice fields.

items.f: Lonar Lake, Maharashtra
items.b: SALTY. The lake fills a crater made by a meteorite. It has no outlet, so the salts have built up.

items.f: The Gangotri glacier, Uttarakhand
items.b: FRESH. A glacier is made from snow, and snow forms from water vapour. The salt stayed in the sea.

items.f: An iceberg near Antarctica
items.b: FRESH. An iceberg is a piece broken off a glacier or an ice sheet. It is made from old snow.

items.f: Sea ice that froze from sea water this winter
items.b: IN BETWEEN. Freezing leaves most of the salt out. But small pockets of very salty water are trapped in the ice.

items.f: Rain falling on Kochi
items.b: FRESH. Only water evaporates from the sea. The salt stays behind.

items.f: A village well near Thanjavur
items.b: FRESH. This is groundwater: rain and river water that soaked into the soil of the Kaveri delta.

items.f: A borewell beside the beach near Chennai, pumped hard for years
items.b: IN BETWEEN. So much fresh water was pumped out that sea water crept in under the ground.

items.f: A creek among the mangroves of the Sundarbans
items.b: IN BETWEEN. River water and the sea's tide mix here twice a day.

items.f: The Dead Sea, between Jordan and Israel
items.b: SALTY. About 340 grams of salt in a litre, nearly ten times as salty as the ocean. No river flows out.

items.f: Lake Baikal, Russia
items.b: FRESH. It is the deepest lake in the world. It holds about a fifth of the fresh water in all the world's lakes and rivers.

items.f: The Caspian Sea
items.b: IN BETWEEN. It is called a sea, but it is a lake with no outlet. It is less than half as salty as the ocean.

items.f: Your tears
items.b: IN BETWEEN. Tears, like blood, hold about 9 grams of salt in a litre. That is about a quarter as salty as the sea.

items.f: The Periyar river, Kerala
items.b: FRESH. River water is rain that has run off the land. It holds only a small part of a gram of salts in a litre.

items.f: The Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, in summer
items.b: SALTY. The sea and the rivers flood this flat land in the monsoon. Then the water evaporates and leaves a white crust of salt.

items.f: Water in a salt pan at Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu
items.b: SALTY. It is sea water that has lost much of its water to the Sun, so it is far saltier than the sea.

items.f: Snow on Kanchenjunga, Sikkim
items.b: FRESH. Snow forms in clouds from water vapour. No salt comes up with the vapour.

items.f: The Red Sea
items.b: SALTY. About 40 grams of salt in a litre. The air is hot and dry and almost no rivers flow in, so it is saltier than the ocean.

printables.title: 3 heading cards
items: FRESH: less than 1 gram of salt in a litre
IN BETWEEN (brackish): saltier than fresh water, less salty than the sea
SALTY: as salty as the sea, or saltier

rules: Lay the 3 heading cards in a row. Shuffle the 24 water cards and put them in a pile, name side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say FRESH, SALTY or IN BETWEEN, and give a reason.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud.
If your heading was right, keep the card. If not, put it under the heading where it belongs.
A right heading with a right reason earns one more turn. You may take only one extra turn at a time.
The game ends when the pile is empty. The player who kept the most cards wins.
Playing alone? Sort all 24 cards under the headings first. Then turn them over and count how many are right. Play again another day and try to beat your score.

good: No river flows out of it.

check.q: A lake has a river flowing in and no river flowing out. What happens to its water over many years?

good: They are places where fresh water and sea water meet.
River water mixes with sea water there.
Some salt was left out or some sea water got in.

games.title: Sea to Glass: a board game of losing and gaining salt
games.context: This is a board game for 1 to 4 players. Each player is a drop of water who starts in the sea, carrying salt. The drop must lose the salt, travel over the land and reach a drinking glass three times.

printables.title: 24 squares for the board. Cut them out and lay them in a ring, in order
items: 1. OPEN SEA. Start here. You are a drop of sea water, and you carry salt.
2. DEEP SEA. You sink into cold, dark water. Nothing changes.
3. WARM SEA SURFACE. The Sun evaporates you. Leave your salt here. Jump to square 9.
4. A SEA TURTLE drinks you. She pushes your salt out through glands near her eyes. You stay in the sea.
5. POLAR SEA. You freeze into sea ice. Miss one turn. Then the ice melts back into the sea.
6. TROPICAL SEA IN MAY. The Sun evaporates you. Leave your salt here. Jump to square 9.
7. SEA-WATER PLANT NEAR CHENNAI. Pumps push you through a very fine filter. Leave your salt here. Jump to square 18.
8. OCEAN CURRENT. The current carries you round. Your next move starts again from square 1.
9. CLOUD. You are fresh water now. You have no salt.
11. SNOW ON A GLACIER. You are ice. Stay here until you roll a 5 or a 6.
12. GAUMUKH. The glacier melts, and you become river water.
14. LAKE. You rest in a fresh lake. Nothing changes.
15. SOIL. You soak into the ground.
16. GROUNDWATER. You move slowly between the grains. On your next turn, move only 1 square.
18. TAP. You run through a pipe into a home.
19. GLASS. Somebody drinks you. Every fresh drop that reaches or passes this square takes one bean.
20. DRAIN. Used water flows on towards the river.
21. RIVER AGAIN. Take a question card.
22. DELTA. The river splits into many channels near the sea.
23. ESTUARY. You float on top of the salt water for a while. You are still fresh.
24. RIVER MOUTH. You mix into the sea. Pick up your salt. Your next move starts from square 1.

printables.title: 12 two-sided question cards (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Out of 1,000 parts of Earth's water, about how many are fresh?
items.b: About 25. The other 975 are salty.

items.f: Where is most of Earth's fresh water?
items.b: Frozen in glaciers and ice sheets. About 17 of the 25 fresh parts are ice.

items.f: Which holds more fresh water: all the lakes and rivers, or the groundwater?
items.b: The groundwater. It holds about 100 times as much.

items.f: Why is rain fresh, when most of it rose from the salty sea?
items.b: Only water evaporates. The salt stays in the sea.

items.f: When sea water freezes, where does most of the salt go?
items.b: It stays in the liquid water that is left. The ice holds much less salt.

items.f: Is an iceberg fresh or salty? Why?
items.b: Fresh. An iceberg is glacier ice, and glacier ice is made from snow.

items.f: Why does drinking sea water make a person thirstier?
items.b: The kidneys need more water to remove the salt than the sea water brought in.

items.f: Fresh water is poured gently on to very salty water. Which one ends up on top?
items.b: The fresh water. It is lighter, so it floats.

items.f: Why does a lake with no river flowing out become salty?
items.b: Water leaves only by evaporation, and the salt stays behind and builds up.

items.f: Name the three forms of water.
items.b: Solid ice, liquid water and water vapour, which is a gas.

items.f: What is brackish water, and where is it found?
items.b: Water saltier than fresh water but less salty than the sea. It is found where rivers meet the sea.

items.f: Name one animal who can live by drinking sea water, and say how.
items.b: An albatross, a gull, a penguin or a sea turtle. Salt glands near the eyes remove the salt.

rules: Lay the 24 squares in a ring, in order. Squares 1 to 8 are the sea. Squares 9 to 24 are the sky and the land.
Each player needs a button for a drop and a grain of rice for the drop's salt. You also need one die and about 12 beans.
Everyone starts on square 1, with the grain of rice beside the button. A drop with rice is salty.
On your turn, roll the die and move forward that many squares. Then do what your square says.
A salty drop cannot leave the sea by moving. If a salty drop would pass square 8, it goes on counting from square 1.
A drop leaves the sea only from square 3, 6 or 7. Leave the rice on that square and jump as the square says.
On a question square, another player reads you the top question card. If you answer well, move 2 more squares. Then put the card under the pile.
Each time your fresh drop reaches or passes square 19, take one bean. A person has had a drink.
When your drop reaches or passes square 24, your move ends there. Take your grain of rice back. Next turn, count on from square 1.
The first player with 3 beans wins.
Playing alone? Count how many turns you need to win 3 beans. Play again and try to need fewer.

check.q: In Sea to Glass, a drop leaves its salt behind on three squares. What happens on two of them?
check.why: On squares 3 and 6 the Sun evaporates the drop, and only water rises into the air. On square 7 a filter holds the salt back. If you chose the river, remember that rivers carry fresh water to the sea, where it picks salt up.

flow.parent: A drop can circle the sea for several turns. That is part of the lesson: most water stays in the sea for a very long time. If a child gets restless, let a salty drop on square 8 roll again.

flow.kid: Where did your drop wait longest? Where did every fresh drop end up?

good: Back in the sea.
At the river mouth, where it picked up salt again.

ask.q: Where did drops wait a long time?
good: In the sea, going round and round.
On the glacier, as ice.
In the groundwater, moving slowly.

experiments.title: Freeze the Sea: does ice leave the salt behind?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make water nearly as salty as the sea and freeze about half of it. Then you taste the melted ice and the liquid that did not freeze. It shows where the salt goes when salt water freezes.
experiments.question: A bowl of salty water is left in the freezer until about half of it is ice. Is the ice as salty as the liquid that is left? Does salty water freeze as soon as plain water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which will taste saltiest: the water you started with, the melted ice, or the liquid left over? Which bowl will show ice first, plain or salty? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two bowls of the same size and material. Put the same amount of water in each, and put both on the same freezer shelf at the same time. Only one thing differs: bowl B has salt. For the tasting, use the same size of drop each time, and rinse your mouth with plain water between drops. The taster must not know which drop is which.
results_table: Saltiness rank from taster 1 (1 is least salty)

materials.item: small steel bowls or steel dabbas of the same size, about 10 cm wide
a 200 ml tumbler
table salt, 1 level teaspoon
a teaspoon and a tablespoon
small katoris, labelled START, ICE and LEFT OVER
a tea strainer
a freezer
paper labels or a marker, a clock, a notebook and a pencil
a tumbler of plain drinking water for rinsing the mouth

experiments.safety: Use clean bowls and drinking water, because you will taste drops of it. Taste one drop at a time and do not drink the salty water.

schedule.what: Morning: make the salt water and put both bowls in the freezer. Look every half hour after the first hour. After 2 to 4 hours, separate the ice from the liquid, taste both and write the results.

experiments.record: Write the time when ice first showed in each bowl. Then fill in the table for START, ICE and LEFT OVER. Under the table, write one sentence that says where the salt went.
