flow.do: 1. Label the bowls A and B. 2. Pour 1 tumbler of water into each. 3. Stir 1 level teaspoon of salt into bowl B until the water is clear. 4. Put 2 tablespoons from bowl B into the katori marked START. 5. Ask for the guesses and the reasons, and write them down.
flow.say: Bowl B is now nearly as salty as the sea. We will freeze about half of it. Which will taste saltiest: this water, the ice, or the liquid left over? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make bowl B salty. Save two spoons as START. Which will be saltiest? Why?

ask.q: Which bowl do you think will show ice first, and why?
good: The plain one, because nothing is in the way.
The salty one will be slower. People put salt on icy roads.
Both at once, because the freezer is equally cold.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect the ice to be as salty as the water, because the salt is spread all through it. Keep the START katori covered on the counter.
flow.context: This is the first step of Freeze the Sea. You make water nearly as salty as the sea and guess where the salt will go when it freezes.

flow.do: Put both bowls on the same freezer shelf and write the time. Look after one hour, and then every 30 minutes, without moving them. Write which bowl shows ice first.
flow.say: Look at both bowls. Is there ice in bowl A? Is there ice in bowl B? What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Look every half hour. Which bowl has ice first? Write the time.
flow.wait: Look every half hour after the first hour. Go on when about half of bowl B is ice, after 2 to 4 hours.
flow.parent: Plain water usually has an ice skin within an hour. The salty bowl starts later, because salt water freezes at about minus 2 degrees. Its ice is often soft and slushy. Take bowl B out when you judge that about half is ice. If it has frozen solid, see the note in the next step.
flow.context: In this step of Freeze the Sea both bowls are in the freezer. You look each hour to see which bowl freezes first.

flow.do: 1. Take bowl B out. Break up the ice with a spoon. 2. Pour everything through the strainer into the LEFT OVER katori. 3. Hold the strainer of ice under a thin stream of tap water for 3 seconds. 4. Tip the ice into the ICE katori. Stand the katori in a bowl of warm water until the ice melts.
flow.say: The strainer holds the ice, and the katori holds the liquid that did not freeze. We rinse the ice for three seconds only. Why do you think we rinse it?
flow.kid: Strain off the liquid. Rinse the ice for three seconds. Let the ice melt.

ask.q: Why do we rinse the ice quickly before melting it?
good: Salty liquid is clinging to the outside of the ice.
We want to taste the ice itself, not the liquid on it.

flow.parent: If bowl B froze solid, do this. Put the whole block in the strainer over the LEFT OVER katori and let it thaw for 15 minutes. The first drips are the saltiest part. Then melt the ice that remains in the ICE katori.
flow.context: In this step of Freeze the Sea you separate the ice from the liquid that did not freeze, and you melt the ice.

flow.do: Your child closes their eyes. Put one drop of START, ICE or LEFT OVER on a clean teaspoon and let them taste it. Do all three in a mixed order. They rinse with plain water between drops. Then they name the least salty and the saltiest. Swap places, so that your child tests you.
flow.say: Close your eyes. I will give you three drops, and I will not say which is which. Tell me which is least salty and which is saltiest.
flow.kid: Close your eyes and taste three drops. Rinse between drops. Which is least salty?

check.q: In Freeze the Sea, why must the taster not know which drop is which?
options: So a guess cannot change what they taste
check.why: A person who expects the ice to be fresh may taste it as fresh. Not knowing keeps the judgement honest. Scientists call this a blind test. If you chose another answer, think about what you expected before you tasted.

flow.parent: Most tasters find LEFT OVER clearly the saltiest and ICE the least salty. The melted ice usually still tastes a little salty. If two samples seem alike, taste that pair again.
flow.context: In this step of Freeze the Sea you taste the three samples without knowing which is which, and you rank them by saltiness.

flow.do: Measure the ICE water and the LEFT OVER liquid in tablespoons. Fill in the table with both tasters' ranks.
flow.say: How many tablespoons of melted ice are there? How many of leftover liquid? Write both tasters' ranks in the table.
flow.kid: Measure both in tablespoons. Write the ranks in your table.
flow.parent: One tumbler holds about 13 tablespoons. Some water is lost in rinsing and straining, so the two parts will not add up exactly.
flow.context: In this step of Freeze the Sea you measure the melted ice and the leftover liquid and fill in the table.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they tasted, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. The salt did not leave the bowl. So where is it now?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you tasted. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The leftover liquid tastes saltier than the water you started with. Where did the extra salt come from?
good: From the water that froze. The ice left its salt behind.
The same salt is now in less water.

ask.q: Why does the melted ice still taste a little salty?
good: Some salty liquid was trapped inside the ice.
The rinse did not remove all the salty liquid.

flow.parent: The reason: in ice, water particles lock together in a regular pattern, and salt does not fit into it. So the growing ice takes water and leaves salt in the liquid, which gets saltier. Saltier water freezes at a lower temperature, so bowl B froze later than bowl A. Some salty liquid is trapped in small pockets in the ice, so the ice is fresher but not fresh. Sea ice in the Arctic forms in the same way.
flow.think: People of the Arctic choose old sea ice to melt for drinking, and not new sea ice. Why might old ice be fresher?
flow.context: This is the last step of Freeze the Sea. You say what the tasting shows about where salt goes when salt water freezes.

experiments.title: The Potato Test: what does salty water do to living cells?
experiments.context: In this experiment thin sticks of raw potato sit for one hour in plain water, in water as salty as the sea and in very salty water. You measure the sticks and bend them. It shows why drinking sea water dries out a body.
experiments.question: Sticks of raw potato sit for one hour in plain water, in home sea water and in very salty water. Which sticks stay stiff and which go limp? Do any change in length?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After one hour, which stick will be stiffest and which will bend most easily? Will any stick get longer or shorter? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Cut all six sticks from one potato, to the same length and thickness. Use the same amount of water in each tumbler, and leave all the sticks in for the same time. Only the amount of salt differs. Put two sticks in each tumbler, because one stick alone could be odd.
results_table: Bend test: snaps, bends a little, or bends into a curve

materials.item: a large raw potato
a knife and a chopping board, for the grown-up
a ruler marked in millimetres
tumblers of 200 ml, labelled PLAIN, SEA and VERY SALTY
table salt, 5 level teaspoons
a teaspoon, a clock, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Nobody eats the raw potato sticks or drinks the salty water.

schedule.what: Cut and measure six potato sticks, and put two in each tumbler. One hour later, measure and bend them, and say what happened.

experiments.record: Fill in the table, with one row for each tumbler. Use the average of the two sticks. Draw the three sticks being bent.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Six thin sticks of raw potato, each about as thick as a pencil, lined up against a ruler on a chopping board.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts 6 sticks, each 60 mm long and as thick as a pencil. Measure each one.

setup.art: Three tumblers of water labelled PLAIN, SEA and VERY SALTY, with two potato sticks standing in each.
setup.caption: 2. Put 2 sticks in plain water, 2 in home sea water and 2 in very salty water. Wait 1 hour.

setup.art: A child's hands gently bending a limp potato stick into a curve, beside a stiff stick that has snapped in two.
setup.caption: 3. Measure each stick again. Bend each one gently and see what it does.

flow.do: Show your child the potato and the three labelled tumblers. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: A potato is made of living cells, and each cell is a tiny bag of watery liquid. Which stick will be stiffest after an hour? Which will bend most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three waters, six potato sticks. Which stick will bend most? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Many children expect the salty sticks to swell, because they are sitting in water. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Potato Test. You guess what plain water and salty water will do to sticks of raw potato.

flow.do: 1. Fill each tumbler with water. 2. Stir 1 level teaspoon of salt into SEA and 4 into VERY SALTY. 3. Peel the potato and cut 6 sticks, each 60 mm long and as thick as a pencil. 4. Your child measures each stick and writes the length. 5. Put 2 sticks in each tumbler and write the time.
flow.say: Measure each stick in millimetres before it goes in. Why do we put two sticks in each tumbler, and not one?
flow.kid: Measure each stick in millimetres. Put two sticks in each tumbler.

ask.q: Why two sticks in each tumbler?
good: One stick could be odd, or cut badly.
If both sticks do the same, we can trust the result more.

flow.wait: Leave the sticks in the water for 1 hour.
flow.parent: Thin sticks matter. A stick as thick as a finger changes too slowly to show much in an hour. If your salt is coarse, stir until no grains are left.
flow.context: In this step of the Potato Test a grown-up cuts six potato sticks. You measure them and put two in each tumbler.

flow.do: After 1 hour, lift out the sticks, one tumbler at a time. Measure each stick. Then hold a stick at both ends and bend it gently. Write whether it snaps, bends a little or bends into a curve.
flow.say: Measure each stick again. Now bend it gently between your fingers. Does it snap, or does it bend? Tell me what you feel.
flow.kid: Measure each stick again. Bend it gently. Does it snap or bend?

check.q: In the Potato Test, the stick from very salty water bends like rubber. What has happened inside the stick?
options: Water has left the potato's cells
The potato has soaked up extra water
check.why: Each cell lost water to the salty water outside, so the cells went slack and the stick went limp. If you chose 'soaked up extra water', look at the plain-water stick. That stick took water in, and it is the stiffest of all.

flow.parent: Expect the plain-water sticks to be crisp and to snap. The sea-water sticks bend a little. The very salty sticks bend into a curve and are a few millimetres shorter. The length changes are small, so the bend test is the clearer result.
flow.context: In this step of the Potato Test the sticks have been in the water for one hour. You measure them again and bend them.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which way did the water move in each tumbler?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Which way did water move in the very salty tumbler? What is your evidence?
good: Out of the potato. The stick got shorter and limp.
Towards the saltier side.

flow.parent: The reason: each potato cell is a bag of slightly salty liquid inside a thin skin. Water passes through the skin easily, and salt does not. Water moves through the skin towards the saltier side. This is called osmosis. In very salty water, water leaves the cells and they go slack. In plain water, water enters the cells and they swell tight, so the stick is stiff.
flow.context: In this step of the Potato Test you say which way the water moved, and you hear the reason.

flow.do: Now link the result to drinking sea water. Ask the question below, and then read the numbers in the note.
flow.say: Your body is made of cells too. What do you think happens to your cells if you drink sea water?
flow.kid: Your body is made of cells too. What would sea water do to them?

ask.q: What happens to a person's cells if they drink sea water?
good: The blood gets saltier, and water leaves the cells.
The cells shrink, like the cells of the potato stick.
The person gets thirstier.

flow.parent: The numbers: blood holds about 9 grams of salt in a litre, and sea water about 35. Human urine can hold only about 20. So the kidneys need more than a litre of water to remove the salt in a litre of sea water. A person who drinks sea water loses water.
flow.think: A sea turtle drinks sea water every day. What must her body be able to do that yours cannot?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Potato Test. You use the result to explain why people cannot drink sea water.

experiments.title: Ice on Land, Ice on Sea: which melting ice raises the water?
experiments.context: In this experiment you melt ice cubes that float in water in one tumbler, and ice cubes that sit above the water in another. You mark the water level before and after. It shows which kind of ice raises the sea when it melts.
experiments.question: Two tumblers hold the same amount of water. In one, ice floats in the water. In the other, ice sits above the water on a strainer. When all the ice has melted, does the water level change in either tumbler?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After the ice melts, will the water be higher, lower or the same in each tumbler? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two clear tumblers of the same size, the same amount of water at the same warmth, and the same number of ice cubes from one tray. Only the place of the ice differs: it floats in tumbler A and sits on a strainer above the water in tumbler B. Mark both water levels before the ice melts.
results_table: Water level before the ice melted
Water level after the ice melted

materials.item: clear straight-sided tumblers of the same size, about 7 cm wide and 10 cm tall
a tea strainer wide enough to rest across the top of a tumbler
ice cubes from one tray, 8 in all
a measuring cup or a tumbler, and a tablespoon
two rubber bands or a marker pen, to mark the water level
a ruler marked in millimetres
a clock, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Wipe up any spilled water at once, so that nobody slips.

schedule.what: Make the ice cubes the night before. Then set up both tumblers, wait about an hour for the ice to melt, measure the change and say what you found.

experiments.record: Draw both tumblers before and after, with the water line. Fill in the table. Under it, write one sentence that says which ice raised the water, and one that says why.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: A: ice floating in the water
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers will be different, but one tumbler should stay level and the other should rise.

setup.art: Two clear tumblers side by side. In tumbler A, four ice cubes float in water. In tumbler B, four ice cubes sit in a tea strainer resting on the rim, above the water. A rubber band marks the water line on each.
setup.caption: 1. Tumbler A: float 4 cubes in the water. Tumbler B: put 4 cubes in a strainer above the water. Mark both water lines.

setup.art: The same two tumblers after an hour, with the ice gone. The water in tumbler A is at its band and the water in tumbler B is clearly above its band.
setup.caption: 2. Wait until all the ice has melted. Look at both water lines.

setup.art: A ruler held beside tumbler B measuring the gap between the rubber band and the new water line in millimetres.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how far each water line has moved from its band.

flow.do: Show your child the two tumblers, the strainer and the ice. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Ice floats in one tumbler and sits above the water in the other. When all of it has melted, which water will be higher? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Ice floats in tumbler A. Ice sits above tumbler B. Which one will rise? Why?
flow.parent: Many children say both rise, because melting adds water. Some say neither. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ice on Land, Ice on Sea. You guess which tumbler of water will rise when the ice melts.

flow.do: 1. Pour 150 ml of water into tumbler A. Use lukewarm tap water for both tumblers. 2. Put 4 ice cubes into tumbler A. 3. Put a rubber band round tumbler A at the water line, or mark the line with a pen. 4. Pour water into tumbler B until it reaches the same height as the band on A. 5. Mark B in the same way.
flow.say: Tumbler A has ice floating in it. We fill tumbler B to the same height, with no ice in it. Why must both lines start at the same height?
flow.kid: Add 4 cubes to tumbler A. Mark its water line. Fill B to the same height. Mark it.

ask.q: Why must both water lines start at the same height?
good: So we can tell which one rose and which did not.
To make it a fair test.

flow.parent: The ice in A pushes the water up as it floats, so B needs more water than A to reach the same line. That is why you fill B to the band, and do not pour 150 ml into each. A 150 ml pour reaches about 4 cm in a tumbler 7 cm wide.
flow.context: In this step of Ice on Land, Ice on Sea you set up tumbler A with floating ice and mark the water line on both tumblers.

flow.do: Rest the strainer across the top of tumbler B. Put 4 ice cubes in the strainer. Check that the bottom of the strainer is at least 1 cm above the water. If it is not, pour a little water out of tumbler B and mark the line again. Write the time. Leave both tumblers in a warm room, out of the Sun's glare.
flow.say: These cubes are above the water, like the ice on top of a mountain. Where will the water from this ice go when it melts?
flow.kid: Put 4 cubes in the strainer above B. Write the time. Wait.
flow.wait: Wait about 45 to 60 minutes, until no ice is left in either tumbler.
flow.parent: In a warm Indian room, 4 cubes melt in about 30 to 60 minutes. The ice in tumbler A melts a little sooner, because it sits in water. If ice is still left after an hour, wait until it has all gone. Do not measure before then.
flow.context: In this step of Ice on Land, Ice on Sea you put the second set of ice cubes above the water in tumbler B, and wait for the ice to melt.

flow.do: When no ice is left, look at both tumblers from the side, with your eyes level with the water line. Hold the ruler against the glass. Measure the gap between each band and the new water line, in millimetres. Fill in the table.
flow.say: Put your eyes level with the water. Is the water in A still at its band? What about B? Measure each gap in millimetres.
flow.kid: Look from the side. Measure how far each water line moved.

check.q: In Ice on Land, Ice on Sea, which tumbler's water rose when the ice melted?
options: Tumbler B, with the ice above the water
Tumbler A, with the floating ice
Both rose by the same amount
check.why: The melted water from the strainer ice was new water added to tumbler B, so its level rose. The floating ice in A was already pushing aside its own weight of water, so the water level stayed put. If you chose both, remember that A's ice was already in the water before it melted.

flow.parent: Tumbler A should stay within 1 or 2 millimetres of its band. Tumbler B should rise by about 10 to 20 millimetres. If A has dropped a little, some water has evaporated or clung to the glass. A change of 1 or 2 millimetres is too small to count.
flow.context: In this step of Ice on Land, Ice on Sea the ice has melted. You measure how far each water line has moved from its band.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which tumbler is like the sea ice, and which is like an ice sheet on land?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Tumbler A is like sea ice. Why did its water not rise?
good: The ice was already in the water, pushing aside water.
The ice turned into just enough water to fill the space it took up.

ask.q: Which ice is like the ice on Antarctica, and what would it do to the sea?
good: The ice above the water, in tumbler B.
It would add water to the sea and raise it.

flow.parent: The reason: a floating cube pushes aside as much water as the whole cube weighs. When it melts, it turns into just that much water, and fills the space. Ice above the water has pushed nothing aside. Its melt water is new water, so the level rises. Ice sheets on Antarctica and Greenland sit on land, like ice in the strainer. Sea ice floats already, like the cubes in A. Warm sea water also takes up a little more room, and this raises the sea too. Real sea water is salty, so floating ice makes a very small change, which can be ignored here.
flow.think: A glacier slides off the land into the sea. At what moment does it start to raise the sea: when it slides in, or later when it melts?
flow.context: This is the last step of Ice on Land, Ice on Sea. You say why the floating ice did not raise the water and the ice above the water did.

activities.title: One Litre Earth: how much of the world's water is fresh?
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. A one-litre bottle stands for all the water on Earth. You measure out the fresh water with a teaspoon and share it between ice, groundwater, and lakes and rivers.

materials.item: a clean 1-litre bottle, full of water
a teaspoon, 5 ml
a small steel katori
a drinking straw
a dark plate
4 paper labels and a pencil

activities.record: Draw the bottle, the katori and the three heaps on the plate. Write the number of teaspoons or drops under each.

setup.art: A one-litre bottle of water with a label that says EARTH, a teaspoon and a small steel katori beside it on a kitchen counter.
setup.caption: 1. The full bottle is all the water on Earth. Take 5 level teaspoons out of it into the katori.

setup.art: A dark plate with a heap of three and a half teaspoons of water labelled ICE, a heap of one and a half teaspoons labelled GROUNDWATER, and one tiny drop labelled LAKES AND RIVERS.
setup.caption: 2. Share the 5 teaspoons. Put 3 and a half on the plate as ICE, and 1 and a half as GROUNDWATER.

setup.art: A child dipping a drinking straw into a katori, with a finger over the top, and letting one drop fall on the dark plate.
setup.caption: 3. Lift one drop with the straw. It stands for all the fresh lakes and rivers in the world.

flow.do: Hold up the full bottle. Say that it stands for all the water on Earth. Ask the question below, and write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: This bottle is all the water on Earth. How many teaspoons of it are fresh water that people can drink? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The bottle is all of Earth's water. How many teaspoons are fresh? Why?

ask.q: Do you think fresh water is a large share or a small share of all the water?
good: Small, because the sea is salty.
A large share, because there are so many rivers.
Any guess with a reason.

flow.parent: Many children guess half a bottle or more, because the Earth looks so wet. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Litre Earth. You guess how much of Earth's water is fresh.

flow.do: 1. Use the teaspoon to take 5 level teaspoons from the bottle. 2. Tip them into the katori. 3. Label the katori FRESH. 4. Say that the water left in the bottle is salty.
flow.say: These 5 teaspoons are all the fresh water on Earth. Everything left in the bottle is salty. How does that look to you?
flow.kid: Take 5 level teaspoons from the bottle. They are all the fresh water.

check.q: In One Litre Earth, how much of the bottle is fresh water?
check.why: Out of every 1,000 parts of Earth's water, about 25 are fresh. The bottle holds 1,000 millilitres, so about 25 millilitres are fresh, which is 5 teaspoons. If you chose a larger amount, remember that nearly all of Earth's water is salty.

flow.parent: A level teaspoon holds 5 ml, so 5 teaspoons make 25 ml. The shares are rounded, so a little more or less is fine.
flow.context: In this step of One Litre Earth you take out the fresh water. It is a very small part of the bottle.

flow.do: 1. Tip 3 and a half teaspoons from the katori on to the dark plate. Label them ICE. 2. Tip 1 and a half teaspoons on to the plate, apart from the ice. Label them GROUNDWATER. 3. Dip the straw in the katori, put a finger on top and lift out one drop. 4. Put the drop on the plate. Label it LAKES AND RIVERS.
flow.say: Most of the fresh water is frozen. Some is under the ground. All the fresh lakes and rivers in the world are this one drop.
flow.kid: Share the 5 teaspoons. Make heaps for ice and groundwater. Add one drop.
flow.parent: A few drops stay in the katori. They stand for frozen soil, the water in the air, and the water in living bodies. The drop for lakes and rivers is not exact, because one drop is about a twentieth of a millilitre.
flow.context: In this step of One Litre Earth you share the fresh water between ice, groundwater, and lakes and rivers.

flow.do: Look at the plate. Ask the questions below, and listen to the answers before you say anything.
flow.say: Look at the three heaps. Which of them can a person reach and drink today? Which is the one that most cities use?
flow.kid: Look at the plate. Which water can you reach and drink?

ask.q: Which of the three heaps can people reach and drink today?
good: Groundwater, through wells and borewells.
The one drop of lakes and rivers.
Ice is frozen and far from most people.

ask.q: Why is it a problem that most cities depend on the one drop?
good: It is so small.
Many people share it, and it can be polluted or dry up.

flow.parent: Many cities also use groundwater, and some use sea water made fresh. Only 25 parts in every 1,000 of Earth's water are fresh, and most of that is hard to reach.
flow.think: The sea is nearly the whole bottle. Why can a person with the sea all around them still run out of water to drink?
flow.context: This is the last step of One Litre Earth. You think about which fresh water people can really use.

activities.title: One Bottle, Three Forms: freeze it, melt it and find the same water
activities.context: In this activity you freeze a cup of water and see if the ice is above the water line. You melt it and see if the line comes back. Then you leave the cup open to see what happens to some of the water. It shows the three forms of one water.

materials.item: a clean plastic cup or a small plastic bottle with the top cut off, 5 to 7 cm wide. Do not use glass
water
a strip of tape or a marker pen
a ruler marked in millimetres
a freezer
a glass of water and one ice cube
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Use only plastic in the freezer. A grown-up cuts the bottle, if you use one.

schedule.what: Fill the cup with water to a line, mark the line, and put the cup in the freezer for the night.
Mark and measure where the top of the ice is. Let the ice melt, and mark the water line again. Leave the cup open.
Mark the water line a third time. Say where the water that is missing went.

activities.record: Draw the cup three times: full of water, full of ice, and melted. Mark each line, and write the heights in millimetres.

setup.art: A clear plastic cup with water filled to a tape mark 8 centimetres up from the bottom, in front of an open freezer.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the cup with water to a line 8 cm from the bottom. Mark the line. Put the cup in the freezer for the night.

setup.art: The same cup the next morning, with a bump of white ice rising above the tape mark and a second tape mark at the top of the bump.
setup.caption: 2. Next day, mark the top of the ice and measure how far it is above the first line.

setup.art: The cup after the ice has melted, with the water back at the first tape mark, standing open on a window sill.
setup.caption: 3. Let the ice melt. Look at the water line. Leave the cup open for another day and look again.

flow.do: Show your child the cup, and ask the question below. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: We will freeze this water. After the night, where will the top of the ice be: above the line, at the line or below it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Water freezes into ice. Will the ice be above the line, at it or below? Why?
flow.parent: Many children say the ice will be at the line, because nothing was added. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of One Bottle, Three Forms. You guess what freezing does to the amount of room the water takes up.

flow.do: 1. Pour water into the cup until it is 8 cm deep. 2. Stick tape on the outside at the water line. 3. Drop an ice cube into a glass of water and watch it. 4. Put the cup in the freezer, upright and level, for 8 hours or overnight.
flow.say: Mark the water line with tape. Then put the ice cube in the glass. Does it sink or float? What does that tell you about ice and water?
flow.kid: Mark the water line with tape. Drop an ice cube in a glass. Put the cup in the freezer.
flow.wait: Leave the cup in the freezer overnight, for at least 8 hours.

ask.q: Does the ice cube sink or float? What does that say about ice compared with water?
good: It floats, so a cupful of ice must weigh less than a cupful of water.
The same water must take up more room when it is ice.

flow.parent: Do not put the lid on. The cup may bulge or crack a little, which is why you must use plastic.
flow.context: In this step of One Bottle, Three Forms you fill and mark the cup, test an ice cube, and freeze the cup.

flow.do: Day 2. 1. Take the cup out. 2. Look at the top of the ice from the side. Stick a second piece of tape at the top of the ice. 3. Measure the gap between the two pieces of tape, in millimetres.
flow.say: Look at the top of the ice. Is it above the first line or below it? How many millimetres above? What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Look at the ice. Is it above the line? Measure the gap in millimetres.

check.q: In One Bottle, Three Forms, the ice stands above the water line. What does this show?
options: Ice takes up more room than the water it came from
Ice has more water in it than water does
check.why: No water was added. The same water, now ice, takes up about one tenth more room, so the ice stands higher. If you chose the second answer, remember that nothing went into the cup.

flow.parent: The top of the ice is often a small bump, and it may be 5 to 10 millimetres above the line. A 5 to 7 cm cup gives a clearer result than a wide bowl.
flow.context: In this step of One Bottle, Three Forms the water has frozen. You measure where the top of the ice is.

flow.do: 1. Leave the cup in the room until all the ice has melted. 2. Look at the water line against the first tape. 3. Leave the cup open on a shelf, away from the Sun, for another day. Do not cover it.
flow.say: The ice is now water again. Is the water at the first line? Where did the extra height go?
flow.kid: Let the ice melt. Is the water at the first line again?
flow.wait: Leave the open cup for one more day.
flow.parent: The melted water should come back to the first line, or very close to it. Some drops may stay on the sides of the cup or on the ice that has not yet melted.
flow.context: In this step of One Bottle, Three Forms the ice melts back to water. You look for the first water line.

flow.do: Day 3. Mark the water line a third time and measure the gap below the first tape. Say what you think happened to the missing water.
flow.say: Is the water line lower now? You did not pour anything out. Where did the water go?
flow.kid: Is the water lower than before? Where did it go?

ask.q: The water line is lower and nobody poured any out. Where did the water go?
good: Into the air as water vapour.
It evaporated, so it is a gas now.

flow.parent: Indoors, an open cup may lose 1 to 3 millimetres in a day, more in a hot dry room. Water vapour is the third form, and the air in the room holds it, invisible.
flow.think: You have now seen one water as ice, as liquid and as vapour. Which of the three do you think is most of Earth's water?
flow.context: This is the last step of One Bottle, Three Forms. You find that some water has left the open cup as a gas.

activities.title: The Island Well: draw water from a jar of two layers
activities.context: In this activity you make a jar with blue salty water at the bottom and clear fresh water on top, as under a small island. You draw samples at two depths with a straw. Then you stir the jar once, like a strong pump.

materials.item: a clear tall jar or tumbler, about 7 cm wide and 10 cm tall
table salt, 1 level teaspoon
a tablespoon and a teaspoon
food colour or ink, 3 drops. Strong tea also works
drinking straws
a white plate
a measuring cup or a tumbler for water

activities.safety: Nobody drinks the blue salty water.
activities.record: Draw the jar with its two layers, and mark where you took each straw sample. Colour the sample on the plate. Draw the jar again after stirring.

setup.art: A clear jar with 5 centimetres of blue salty water, and a spoon held upside down touching the glass just above the water while clear water runs slowly over its back.
setup.caption: 1. Make blue salt water in the jar. Pour clear fresh water slowly over the back of a spoon to make a top layer.

setup.art: A drinking straw with a thumb on its top end, lowered into the clear top layer of the jar, and a white plate beside it with one clear drop on it.
setup.caption: 2. Close the top of a straw with your thumb. Lower it 1 cm into the top layer, lift your thumb and close it again. Put the drop on the plate.

setup.art: The same jar after one spoon has stirred it, with the water pale blue all through, and a plate beside it with a pale blue drop.
setup.caption: 3. Take a sample from deeper down. Then stir the jar three times and look again.

flow.do: Show your child the jar, the salt and the clear water. Ask the question below. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Under a small island, rain soaks into the sand and meets the sea water. If we pour clear fresh water on blue salt water, what will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Clear water goes on blue salt water. Will they mix or stay apart? Why?
flow.parent: Many children think they will mix at once, as when a drop of ink goes into a glass. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Island Well. You guess what fresh water does when it is poured on salt water.

flow.do: 1. Stir 1 level teaspoon of salt into 200 ml of water until it is clear. 2. Add 3 drops of food colour. 3. Pour it into the jar. 4. Hold a spoon upside down, touching the glass just above the water. 5. Pour 100 ml of clear water slowly over the back of the spoon.
flow.say: The blue water is as salty as the sea. The clear water has no salt. Pour the clear water as slowly as you can, over the spoon.
flow.kid: Make blue salt water. Pour clear water slowly over a spoon on top.
flow.parent: The two layers should be sharp, with the clear water about 2 to 3 cm deep. If the whole jar goes pale blue, the pouring was too fast. Empty the jar and start again, more slowly.
flow.context: In this step of The Island Well you build the jar with a blue salty layer and a clear fresh layer on top.

flow.do: 1. Close the top of a straw with your thumb. 2. Lower the straw 1 cm into the clear layer. 3. Lift your thumb, count to 3, and close it again. 4. Lift the straw out and let the sample drop on the white plate. 5. Do the same again at the bottom of the jar.
flow.say: Take one sample near the top and one near the bottom. What colour is each one? Which is the water an island family could drink?
flow.kid: Take a sample from the top. Take one from the bottom. What colour is each?

check.q: In The Island Well, a straw takes a sample from the clear top layer. What colour is it?
options: Clear, because it is fresh water
Pale blue, because the layers have mixed
check.why: The fresh water floats on top of the heavier blue salt water, and the two layers stay apart if nobody disturbs them. A top sample is clear. If you chose pale blue, the layers may have mixed because the pouring was too fast.

flow.parent: Do the top sample gently, so that the straw does not drag blue water upward. If the top sample looks blue, the straw went too deep or the layers have mixed.
flow.context: In this step of The Island Well you take straw samples from two depths and compare their colours.

flow.do: Stir the jar three times with a spoon, like a strong pump. Wait 5 minutes. Look at the jar. Then take one sample from the top and put it on the plate.
flow.say: Stir the jar three times. This is like a pump that pulls too hard. What does the top sample look like now?
flow.kid: Stir the jar three times. Wait. Take a top sample. What colour is it?
flow.parent: After the stir the whole jar turns pale blue, and it stays that way. The water is mixed, and the fresh water is no longer fresh.
flow.context: In this step of The Island Well you stir the jar like a strong pump and take a sample from the top again.

flow.do: Look at the jar and the plate together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. How would you take water from an island's fresh layer?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why did the clear water stay on top?
good: It is lighter than salt water.
Salt makes the water heavier.

ask.q: What did the stirring do?
good: It mixed the fresh and salt water, and they do not come apart again.
It spoiled the fresh water.

flow.parent: The reason: a litre of fresh water has a mass of about 1,000 grams, and a litre of sea water about 1,025 grams. The lighter water floats. A layer of fresh water under an island floats in the same way, and a strong pump near the salt layer pulls it upward and mixes it. Only new rain makes fresh water again.
flow.think: In The Well That Moved with the Tide, Ayesha's well rose and fell with the tide. What does that tell you about what lies under the sand?
flow.context: This is the last step of The Island Well. You say why fresh water floats on salt water and why strong pumping spoils the well.

activities.title: Pin the Fresh Water: ten places on a map
activities.context: In this activity you pin ten waters on a world map and an India map: ice, lakes, rivers and groundwater, and some salty waters too. You look at how far each is from where most people live.

materials.item: a world map or an atlas page
a map of India
coloured pencils or stickers in white, blue, green, orange and red
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Make a key with five colours. Write the name of each of the ten places beside its colour. Then write which pins are far from where most people live.

setup.art: A world map on a table with a white dot on Antarctica and a white dot on Greenland, and a child holding a white pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Put a white dot on each place that holds ice: Antarctica, Greenland and the Gangotri glacier.

setup.art: A world map with blue dots on Lake Baikal and the Great Lakes of North America, and a green patch across the Ganga plain in north India.
setup.caption: 2. Put blue dots on the big fresh lakes and a green patch on the groundwater under the Ganga plain.

setup.art: A map of India with an orange dot on Chilika, a red dot on Sambhar Lake, and a blue line along the Kaveri river.
setup.caption: 3. Put an orange dot on a brackish water, a red dot on a salty lake, and trace one river in blue.

flow.do: Show your child the world map. Ask the question below. Write the guess and the reason, and draw a pencil ring where they think most of the fresh water is.
flow.say: Most of Earth's fresh water is in a few places. Where on this map do you think it is? Draw a ring. Why there?
flow.kid: Where is most of Earth's fresh water? Draw a ring. Why there?
flow.parent: Children often ring rivers or lakes. Most of the fresh water is ice, near the poles and on high mountains. Do not correct the guess yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pin the Fresh Water. You guess where Earth's fresh water is, before you pin it.

flow.do: Find each place on the map and mark it. Mark Antarctica, Greenland and the Gangotri glacier in Uttarakhand in white. Mark Lake Baikal in Russia, the Great Lakes of North America and the Kaveri river in blue. Mark the groundwater under the Ganga plain in green. Mark Chilika lagoon in Odisha in orange. Mark Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan and the Dead Sea in red.
flow.say: Take one place at a time. Find it, mark it in its colour, and say what kind of water it holds. Is it ice, fresh, brackish or salty?
flow.kid: Find each place. Mark it in its colour. Say what water it holds.

check.q: In Pin the Fresh Water, which pin shows the largest store of fresh water?
options: White, for the ice on Antarctica
Green, for the Ganga plain's groundwater
check.why: About nine tenths of the world's ice lies on Antarctica, and ice is about two thirds of all fresh water. Lake Baikal holds about a fifth of the world's fresh lake and river water, and groundwater holds about 100 times more than all the lakes and rivers. If you chose Baikal or the groundwater, check the One Litre Earth heaps again.

flow.parent: Use a phone map if the atlas does not show a place. The Great Lakes are on the border of the United States and Canada. The Ganga plain holds one of the great groundwater stores of the world, and many wells and borewells draw on it.
flow.context: In this step of Pin the Fresh Water you find ten waters on the map and mark each one by its kind.

flow.do: Look at the map together. Ask the questions below, and let your child answer from the pins.
flow.say: Look at your white pins. Are they close to where most people live? Which pins are in India? Which kind of pin is the most common?
flow.kid: Look at the white pins. Are they near where people live?

ask.q: Look at the white pins. Are they near where most people live?
good: No, they are at the poles and high in the mountains.
Most of the ice is far from cities.

ask.q: Which pins are in India, and what do they hold?
good: The Gangotri glacier is ice, the Kaveri is fresh, the Ganga plain is groundwater, Chilika is brackish, and Sambhar is salty.

flow.parent: Gangotri and the other Himalayan glaciers feed rivers that millions of people use, so some ice is close to a great many people.
flow.think: Ice in the Himalayas melts into rivers that people use. Ice on Antarctica does not. What difference does that make to how much each store helps people?
flow.context: This is the last step of Pin the Fresh Water. You look at how far the fresh water is from the people who need it.

activities.title: Mix a Lagoon: make water as salty as Chilika in the monsoon and in summer
activities.context: In this activity you mix sea-strength salt water with plain water to make a monsoon lagoon and a summer lagoon. You work out how salty each is, and then taste them without knowing which is which.

materials.item: table salt, 1 level teaspoon
a tumbler of 200 ml, and a tablespoon
small katoris, labelled SEA, MONSOON, SUMMER and PLAIN
a teaspoon for tasting, rinsed between tastes
a tumbler of plain water for rinsing the mouth
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Taste only one drop at a time, and do not drink the salty water.
activities.record: Fill in a table with four rows: PLAIN, MONSOON, SUMMER and SEA. For each row write the spoons of sea water, the grams of salt in a litre and the taster's rank.

setup.art: A tumbler of water with a level teaspoon of salt beside it, and a child stirring the salt in.
setup.caption: 1. Stir 1 level teaspoon of salt into 1 tumbler of water. This is SEA.

setup.art: Four small katoris labelled PLAIN, MONSOON, SUMMER and SEA, with spoons of sea water and plain water going into two of them.
setup.caption: 2. Make MONSOON with 1 spoon of sea water and 9 of plain. Make SUMMER with 5 spoons of each.

setup.art: A child with eyes closed tasting a drop from a teaspoon held by a grown-up, with the four katoris in a mixed order.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up mixes up the katoris. Taste one drop of each and put them in order.

flow.do: Say that Chilika is a lagoon where rivers meet the sea. Ask the question below. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: In the monsoon, rivers pour fresh water into Chilika. In summer, the rivers shrink and the sea comes in. When is Chilika saltier? Why?
flow.kid: When is Chilika saltier, in the monsoon or in summer? Why?
flow.parent: The answer is summer. Children usually guess it right, and the next steps show by how much.
flow.context: This is the first step of Mix a Lagoon. You guess when the lagoon is saltier.

flow.do: 1. Stir 1 level teaspoon of salt into the tumbler of water. Pour 10 tablespoons into the SEA katori. 2. In MONSOON, put 1 tablespoon of sea water and 9 of plain water. 3. In SUMMER, put 5 tablespoons of each. 4. In PLAIN, put 10 tablespoons of plain water.
flow.say: SEA is as salty as the sea. MONSOON has 1 part in 10 of sea water. SUMMER has half. How much salt does each hold?
flow.kid: Make SEA. Make MONSOON with 1 spoon of sea. Make SUMMER with 5 spoons.
flow.parent: One level teaspoon in 200 ml is about 30 grams in a litre. That is close to the sea, which is about 35. Each katori holds 10 tablespoons, which is about 150 ml.
flow.context: In this step of Mix a Lagoon you mix sea-strength water with plain water to make two lagoons.

flow.do: A grown-up mixes up the four katoris. Your child tastes one drop from each, and rinses between drops. Then they put the four in order, from least salty to most salty.
flow.say: I have mixed up the katoris. Taste one drop of each, and rinse between drops. Put them in order from the least salty to the most salty.
flow.kid: Taste one drop from each katori. Rinse between drops. Put them in order.
flow.parent: Most tasters can tell PLAIN from MONSOON only with care, because the difference is small. SUMMER and SEA are clearly salty. If two seem alike, taste that pair again.
flow.context: In this step of Mix a Lagoon you taste the four waters without knowing which is which.

flow.do: Work out the grams of salt in a litre for each katori. SEA holds about 30. MONSOON holds one tenth of that. SUMMER holds half. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: SEA holds about 30 grams in a litre. MONSOON has one tenth of the sea water, so how many grams? SUMMER has half, so how many?
flow.kid: SEA has about 30 grams in a litre. Work out MONSOON and SUMMER.

check.q: In Mix a Lagoon, SUMMER is half sea water and half plain water. About how many grams of salt does a litre of it hold?
check.why: Half of the sea water's 30 grams is 15 grams. A litre of SEA holds 30 grams, so half as much sea water holds half as much salt. If you chose 30, remember that half the water has no salt.

flow.parent: MONSOON works out at 3 grams in a litre. SUMMER works out at 15. Both are brackish, because brackish water is between fresh and the sea. Fresh water has under 1 gram. Real lagoon water changes from place to place and from week to week.
flow.think: A fish that lives in Chilika must cope with water that changes from 3 to 15 grams in a litre in one year. What might her body need to do?
flow.context: This is the last step of Mix a Lagoon. You work out how salty each mix is.

projects.title: The Roof and the Tap: how much water falls on our own home?
projects.context: In this three-day project you work out how many litres of rain fall on your own roof in a year. You compare that with how much water your family uses. It shows how much of a home's water the rain could supply.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a measuring tape, or a long string and a ruler
a calculator, or paper and a grown-up to check the sums
the yearly rain of your town, from a weather website or from the table in the notes

projects.safety: Do not climb on any roof. Measure from the ground or from the plan of the building, or ask a grown-up.

schedule.what: Find out where your home's water comes from and how many litres the family uses in a day.
Find the area of the roof over your home and work out the litres of rain that fall on it in a year.
Compare the rain with the family's use, and write what share the rain could give.

projects.record: A table with five rows: the source of your water, the litres used in a day, the roof area, the rain in a year and the share the roof could give. Add one sentence at the end.

setup.art: A child reading the numbers on a water bill, or the size marked on an overhead tank, with a grown-up beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Find out where the water comes from and how much the family uses in a day.

setup.art: A child with a measuring tape along one side of a flat roof plan drawn on paper, with the length and the width written in metres.
setup.caption: 2. Find the length and width of your roof in metres. Multiply them to get the area.

setup.art: A notebook page with a sum that multiplies roof area by the yearly rain in millimetres, and an arrow to the answer in litres.
setup.caption: 3. Multiply the roof area by the yearly rain in millimetres. The answer is litres.

flow.do: Day 1. 1. Ask where your tap water comes from, for example a lake, a river, a borewell or a tanker. 2. Find the tank size, or the daily use on the water bill. 3. If you cannot find it, use 135 litres for each person each day. 4. Multiply by the number of people at home.
flow.say: Where does our tap water come from? How many litres do we use in a day? Guess first. Then we will find out.
flow.kid: Where does our tap water come from? How many litres do we use each day?
flow.parent: Day 1 answers set up the sum. A common value for a family of 4 is 135 litres for each person, which is 540 litres a day. The real figure may be lower or higher.

ask.q: Where do you think the water in our tap fell as rain?
good: On a lake or river far away, or on the ground above a borewell.

flow.context: This is the first day of The Roof and the Tap. You find where your water comes from and how much your family uses.

flow.do: Day 2. 1. Measure the length and width of the roof over your home in metres. 2. Multiply length by width to get the area in square metres. 3. Find your town's yearly rain in millimetres. 4. Multiply the area by the rain. The answer is litres.
flow.say: One millimetre of rain on one square metre of roof is exactly one litre. How many square metres is our roof? How many litres of rain fall on it in a year?
flow.kid: Work out the roof area. Multiply it by the yearly rain in millimetres.
flow.parent: Why one millimetre on one square metre is one litre: a square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm, which is 10,000 square centimetres. One millimetre is a tenth of a centimetre. 10,000 times 0.1 is 1,000 cubic centimetres, which is 1 litre. In a flat, divide the building's roof area by the number of homes. Rough yearly rain, rounded: Chennai about 1,400 mm, Bengaluru about 900, Mumbai about 2,300, Delhi about 800, Kochi about 3,000, Jaisalmer about 200. Look up your own town if you can.
flow.context: On the second day of The Roof and the Tap you work out how many litres of rain fall on your roof in a year.

flow.do: Day 3. 1. Say that a roof tank catches about 8 tenths of the rain, because some splashes away. Multiply your rain by 8 tenths. 2. Divide by the family's use in a year, which is the daily use times 365. 3. Write the share as a fraction.
flow.say: If we caught 8 tenths of the rain from our roof, what share of the family's water would that be? Is it more than half? Less than half?
flow.kid: Find 8 tenths of your roof's rain. Compare it with the family's yearly use.

check.q: A roof of 100 square metres gets 900 millimetres of rain a year. How many litres fall on it?
check.why: Each square metre gets 900 litres, because one millimetre on one square metre is one litre. 900 litres times 100 square metres is 90,000 litres. If you chose another number, check how many times you multiplied by ten.

flow.parent: With made-up numbers, a 100 square metre roof, 900 mm of rain and 8 tenths caught give 72,000 litres. A family of 4 at 135 litres each uses 540 litres a day, or 197,100 litres a year. The roof could give 72,000 out of 197,100, which is about 4 tenths. It is a large share, and the rest must come from elsewhere.
flow.think: Rain falls in a few weeks, and the family needs water all year. What would the roof's water need, to be useful in the dry months?
flow.context: This is the last day of The Roof and the Tap. You compare the rain on your roof with what your family uses.

challenges.title: Fresher Ice: use freezing to take more salt out
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In Freeze the Sea, the melted ice was fresher than the sea-strength water you began with, but still a little salty. Here you try to make ice that is fresher still.
challenges.problem: Start with 1 tumbler of sea-strength water, made with 1 level teaspoon of salt in 200 ml. Use only a freezer, bowls, a strainer and plain water. Make the freshest melted ice you can. You may freeze it more than once, and you may rinse it.
constraints: Start with the same sea-strength water as Freeze the Sea.
No boiling. Use only freezing, straining and a quick rinse.
You must end with at least 3 tablespoons of melted ice to taste.
A grown-up tastes your sample and the single-freeze ice from Freeze the Sea without knowing which is which. The fresher one wins.
materials: small katoris and teaspoons for tasting
general: Freeze a shallow bowl until it is half ice. Pour off the liquid, rinse the ice quickly, and melt it.
Break the ice into small pieces before you rinse it, so that more of the salty liquid washes away.
Freeze slowly, on a low shelf, and stop at half ice, because the last part to freeze holds the most salt.
creative: Freeze the melted ice a second time, and keep only half of the new ice.
Freeze in a tilted tray, so that the salty liquid runs to one end and can be poured off.
Throw away the first drops and the last drops that come off a thawing block, because they are the saltiest.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way of making fresh ice from salty water. Draw your method, and write the steps. Say how many tablespoons you ended with, and where the salt went.

setup.art: A shallow steel bowl of salty water in a freezer, beside a second bowl that holds the melted ice from the first freeze.
setup.caption: 1. Freeze the sea-strength water until it is about half ice. Pour off the liquid.

setup.art: A child rinsing a strainer of crushed ice under a thin stream of water, and a second bowl waiting beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Rinse the ice quickly, melt it, and freeze it again if your design says so.

setup.art: A grown-up holding up two katoris for a child with closed eyes to taste, with labels hidden underneath.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up gives you two blind tastes. Say which is fresher.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Remember Freeze the Sea. Ask your child for three ideas, and which one they expect to work best.
flow.say: In Freeze the Sea, the ice left most of the salt in the liquid. Some salty liquid stayed in the ice. How could we get rid of more of it? Which idea will work best? Why?
flow.kid: The ice in Freeze the Sea was still a little salty. How could you get it fresher?

ask.q: In Freeze the Sea, why was the melted ice still a little salty?
good: Some salty liquid was trapped in the ice.
Salty liquid clung to the outside of the ice.

flow.parent: The salty liquid is trapped in tiny pockets between the ice crystals. Anything that opens those pockets or drains them, such as breaking the ice, rinsing it or freezing a second time, helps.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fresher Ice. You think of ways to get more salt out of freezing salt water.

flow.do: Choose one design. Make it and write each step. Freeze for as long as it needs, and look every half hour. Write the time of each step.
flow.say: Choose your design. Write down each step before you start. Then do it, and write the times.
flow.kid: Choose a design. Write the steps. Then do it and write the times.
flow.wait: Freezing takes 2 to 4 hours for each round. A second round takes about the same again.
flow.parent: Do the single-freeze version of Freeze the Sea at the same time, so that the two samples are made from the same water. If you want to save time, freeze both on the same shelf.
flow.context: In this step of Fresher Ice you build your design, and freeze and strain your ice.

flow.do: Melt your ice in a clean katori. A grown-up gives your child one drop of each sample, without saying which is which. Your child says which is fresher.
flow.say: I will give you two drops, and I will not say which is which. Which one is fresher? Rinse your mouth between drops.
flow.kid: Taste two drops. Which is fresher? Rinse in between.

check.q: In Fresher Ice, why must the taster not know which sample is which?
options: So a guess cannot change the result
check.why: A taster who expects a double-freeze sample to be fresher might taste it as fresher. Not knowing keeps the result honest. If you chose another answer, think about what a person who knows might expect to taste.

flow.parent: If the two tastes seem equal, your design did not take out more salt than a single freeze. That is a result, and a useful one. Try a different change, and test again.
flow.context: In this step of Fresher Ice a grown-up tastes your ice against the single-freeze ice, without saying which is which.

flow.do: Look at the results together. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Which design made the freshest ice? How much melted ice was left? What do you give up to get fresher ice?
flow.kid: Which design was freshest? How much ice was left?

ask.q: What do you give up to get fresher ice?
good: Less water, because some is thrown away each time.
More time, because each freeze takes hours.

flow.parent: A second freezing leaves less water but fresher. This is how freeze desalination works, in plants that use cold to take the salt out of sea water. It costs a great deal of energy.
flow.context: This is the last step of Fresher Ice. You say which design worked best and what it cost.

challenges.title: A Water Plan for a Small Island
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In The Well That Moved with the Tide, the island families drew sweet water from a thin layer under the sand. Here you plan the water for a made-up island of 300 people.
challenges.problem: A made-up coral island has 300 people. Each person needs 40 litres a day for drinking, cooking and washing. The island has 3,000 square metres of roof and 1,500 millimetres of rain a year. Plan where the water comes from for the whole year.
constraints: The yearly need is 300 people times 40 litres times 365 days.
Roof tanks catch 7 tenths of the rain that falls on the roofs.
The island's shallow wells can safely give 2,000 litres a day in all. More than that turns the water salty.
A sea-water plant makes fresh water at 2,000 litres a day. It uses fuel, and sends salty water back to the sea.
materials: a calculator, or a grown-up to check the sums
general: Collect rain from every roof into tanks, and use the tank water first.
Use the wells for the rest, and never pump more than 2,000 litres a day.
Run the sea-water plant only when the tanks and the wells are not enough.
creative: Flush toilets with sea water, so that fresh water is used only for drinking, cooking and washing.
Use washing water for the coconut palms and the vegetable beds.
Mend leaking pipes and taps first, because a litre that is saved costs nothing to make.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own plan for the island. Draw it, and list the litres from the roofs, the wells and the plant. Say how you would keep the wells from turning salty.
