setup.caption: 1. Draw the island with its roofs, tanks, wells and plant.

setup.art: A notebook page with three sums in a column: rain from the roofs, safe litres from the wells, and the litres the plant must make.
setup.caption: 2. Work out the litres from each source, and add them.

setup.art: A drawing of a shallow well in sand with a thin layer of fresh water floating on blue salty water, and a note about pumping slowly.
setup.caption: 3. Write how you would draw the well water so that it does not turn salty.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Work out how many litres the island needs in a year. Write the sum and the answer.
flow.say: The island has 300 people, and each person needs 40 litres a day. How many litres is that in a day? How many in a year? Which source do you think will give the most?
flow.kid: 300 people use 40 litres each a day. How many litres is that in a year?
flow.parent: 300 times 40 is 12,000 litres a day. 12,000 times 365 is 4,380,000 litres a year.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Water Plan for a Small Island. You find how much water the island needs.

flow.do: Work out each source. 1. Rain on the roofs: 3,000 times 1,500 litres. 2. Multiply by 7 tenths. 3. Wells: 2,000 times 365. 4. Add the two. How many litres are still missing?
flow.say: One millimetre of rain on one square metre is one litre. How many litres of rain fall on all the roofs in a year? How much do the tanks catch? How much can the wells give?
flow.kid: Work out the rain from the roofs. Work out the wells. How much is still missing?

check.q: The island's roofs catch 3,150,000 litres a year, and its wells give 730,000. The need is 4,380,000. Which is true?
options: About 500,000 litres a year are still missing
The island has more than it needs
Exactly the right amount is caught
check.why: 3,150,000 plus 730,000 is 3,880,000 litres. The need is 4,380,000, so 500,000 litres are missing. If you chose the second answer, add the sources again and compare with the need.

flow.parent: Rain on roofs: 3,000 square metres times 1,500 mm is 4,500,000 litres. Seven tenths of that is 3,150,000. Wells: 2,000 times 365 is 730,000. The gap is 500,000 litres a year, which is about 1,400 litres a day.
flow.context: In this step of A Water Plan for a Small Island you add up what the roofs and the wells can give.

flow.do: Decide how to fill the gap. The plant makes 2,000 litres a day. How many days a year must it run? Then draw the plan.
flow.say: How many litres a year are still missing? The plant makes 2,000 litres a day. How many days must it run? What else could close the gap?
flow.kid: Find how many days the plant must run. Draw the plan.
flow.parent: 500,000 divided by 2,000 is 250 days. The plant would run most of the year. Saving water, as in the creative ideas, can cut that. Tanks must also store rain for the dry months, so the roofs' water is not all available at once.
flow.context: In this step of A Water Plan for a Small Island you close the gap and draw your plan.

flow.do: Show the plan to a family member. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Explain your plan. Why do the wells have a limit? What would happen if the island pumped more?
flow.kid: Explain your plan. Why do the wells have a limit?

ask.q: Why do the wells have a limit of 2,000 litres a day?
good: Pumping harder pulls up the salt water that is under the fresh layer.
The fresh layer is thin, and rain refills it slowly.

ask.q: What is the cheapest way to close the gap?
good: Save water first, then use the plant for what is left.
Mend leaks and use water twice.

flow.parent: There is no single right plan. A good plan uses the rain first, keeps the wells below their limit, and runs the plant only for the gap.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Water Plan for a Small Island. You explain your plan and why the wells must not be over-pumped.

items.p: Out of every 1,000 parts of Earth's water, about how many are fresh?
items.why: About 975 parts are salty and about 25 are fresh. That is 2 and a half parts in 100. If you chose a larger number, remember that most of the water is in the salty sea.

items.p: Water with less than 1 gram of salt in a litre is called ____ water.
items.why: Fresh water holds very little dissolved salt. Sea water holds about 35 grams in a litre, and brackish water is in between.

items.p: Match each water to how salty it is.
items.why: Rain holds almost no salt. A lagoon where rivers meet the sea is brackish. The sea holds about 35 grams, and the Dead Sea holds nearly ten times as much, because no river flows out of it.

items.p: Most of Earth's fresh water is in lakes and rivers.
items.why: False. All the fresh lakes and rivers together are only about one drop in One Litre Earth. Most fresh water is ice, and most of the rest is groundwater.

items.p: Where is most of Earth's fresh water?
opts: Frozen in ice sheets and glaciers
items.why: About 17 of the 25 fresh parts are ice, mostly on Antarctica. Rivers, lakes and the air hold far less.

items.p: Put these in order, from the most fresh water to the least:
items.why: Ice holds about 17 parts, groundwater about 7 and a half, and all the fresh lakes and rivers less than one tenth of one part.

items.p: What changes liquid water into water vapour?
items.why: Heat entering a liquid lets its particles fly off as a gas. This is evaporation. Heat leaving the water makes it freeze or the vapour condense.

items.p: Sort each water by its form.
items: The invisible vapour in room air
items.why: Glacier ice, frost and hail are solid water. Rivers and coconut water are liquid. Water vapour is a gas, and it is invisible.

items.p: When salt water freezes, the ice holds all the salt that was in the water.
items.why: False. In Freeze the Sea, the melted ice tasted much less salty than the liquid left in the bowl. Most of the salt stays in the liquid.

items.p: In Freeze the Sea, the leftover liquid tasted saltier than the water you started with. Explain why.
items.a: As the ice grew, it took water and left most of the salt in the liquid. The same salt was then in less water, so the liquid tasted saltier than the start.
items.why: A strong answer says that the ice left salt behind, and that the same salt in less liquid is stronger. It uses what was tasted.

items.p: Rain rose from the salty sea. Why is rain fresh?
opts: Only water evaporates, and the salt stays in the sea
Clouds wash the salt out of the rain
The Sun burns the salt away
items.why: When sea water evaporates, only water particles fly into the air. The salt is left in the sea. So rain, and the rivers it fills, are fresh.

items.p: A person drinks a litre of sea water. What happens to the water in their body?
opts: The body loses more water than it drank
The body gains one litre of water
items.why: To get rid of the salt, the kidneys need more than a litre of the body's own water. So the person ends up with less water than before.

items.p: Draw a potato stick from plain water and one from very salty water, each being bent. Show how each looks.
items.a: The plain-water stick is stiff and snaps or bends only a little. The very salty stick is limp and bends into a curve. Arrows can show water going out of the limp stick.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference between a stiff stick and a limp one, and may show water leaving the cells of the limp stick.
items.art: Two blank boxes labelled PLAIN WATER and VERY SALTY WATER, each with space to draw a bent potato stick.

items.p: Label the three stores of fresh water in One Litre Earth, and write how much each holds.
a: Ice: about 3 and a half teaspoons
Groundwater: about 1 and a half teaspoons
Lakes and rivers: about one drop
items.why: These are the heaps on the plate. Together the ice and the groundwater make nearly all of the 5 teaspoons of fresh water.
items.art: A dark plate with three heaps of water and three blank label lines.

items.p: A coastal village's well has turned salty. What should the village do first?

views.says: Dig the well deeper. Deeper water must be sweeter.
Stop pumping so hard, and catch rain from the roofs. Sea water gets in when too much is pumped out.
Do not drink the water until it is tested. Bring safe water by tanker for now.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you know about wells near the sea. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason: pumping too hard pulls sea water inland under the ground, so digging deeper may make the water saltier. Another: a tanker is a short-term answer, while rain and gentler pumping fix the cause.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that fresh water floats on sea water and that strong pumping mixes them. It treats the other views fairly, since each answers a different part of the problem.

items.p: In Freeze the Sea, the plain bowl showed ice first and the salty bowl later. What is the best reason?
opts: Salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes
Salt water is warmer to begin with
The salty bowl held more water
The freezer was warmer at that bowl
items.why: Sea-strength water starts to freeze at about minus 2 degrees Celsius, while plain water freezes at 0. So the salty bowl had to get colder first.

items.p: Sea water holds about 35 grams of salt in a litre. How many grams are in 4 litres?
items.why: 4 litres hold 4 times 35 grams, which is 140 grams.

items.p: Sea ice and an iceberg are made in the same way.
items.why: False. Sea ice forms when the sea's own surface freezes, so it holds a little salt. An iceberg is a piece of glacier ice that broke off into the sea. It is made from snow, so it is fresh.

items.p: A glacier slides off the land into the sea. When does the sea start to rise?
opts: As soon as the ice is floating in the sea
Only when the ice has fully melted
Never, because ice is already water
items.why: Floating ice pushes aside its own weight of water as soon as it is in the sea. That already raises the level. Melting later changes it very little. This matches what happened to tumbler B.

items.p: In Ice on Land, Ice on Sea, one tumbler rose and the other did not. Say why they were different.
items.a: In tumbler A the ice was already in the water, pushing aside its own weight of water. When it melted, it filled that space, so the level stayed. In tumbler B the ice was above the water, so its melt water was new water and the level rose.
items.why: A strong answer says where the ice was at the start, and that melt water from floating ice fills the room the ice took up, while melt water from ice above adds new water.

items.p: Three of these are fresh water. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Glacier ice, rain and icebergs all began as snow or rain, which are fresh. Sambhar Lake has no river flowing out, so evaporation has left its salt behind.

items.p: Match each living being to the way they get rid of salt.
pairs: A salt gland above each eye drips salty liquid from her beak
Salt glands near the eyes make salty tears
Salt is pushed out through the gills
Salt leaves through the leaves and dries as crystals
items.why: Each has its own way of removing the salt that sea water brings in. Humans cannot do this, which is why people cannot live on sea water.

items.p: Why does a lake with no river flowing out turn salty over many years?
opts: Water leaves only by evaporation, and the salt stays
Rain brings salt down from the clouds
The lake bed makes new salt
items.why: Rivers carry a little dissolved salt into the lake. Water leaves only as vapour, and the salt cannot. So the salt builds up, year after year.

items.p: Is each store of fresh water easy or hard for people to reach?
items: A glacier high in the Karakoram
items.why: People can reach rivers, lakes and wells with a pipe or a bucket. Ice far away, and water deep in rock, are too far or too hard to use.

items.p: Label the three layers under a coral island: fresh water, sea water and dry sand.
a: Fresh water layer: floating in the middle, on the sea water
Sea water: below and around the fresh layer
items.why: Rain soaks through dry sand and floats as a layer on the heavier sea water. A shallow well reaches only the fresh layer.
items.art: A cut-away of a small coral island with three blank label lines pointing to the top, middle and bottom layers.

items.p: Why is a potato stick in very salty water limp after an hour?
opts: Water left its cells towards the saltier side
The stick soaked up the salt
items.why: Water moves through the thin skin of a cell towards the saltier side. The cells lose water and go slack, so the stick bends.

items.p: Some people think a little sea water each day would keep a sailor alive. Explain why it would not.
items.a: Sea water is saltier than the body's liquids. To remove the salt, the kidneys need more water than the sea water brought. So each drink leaves the body with less water, and the sailor gets thirstier.
items.why: A strong answer says that the kidneys can make urine only a little saltier than blood, so they need extra body water to carry the salt out.

items.p: A deeper well always gives fresher water.
items.why: False. Near the sea, the salt water lies under the fresh water. A well that goes too deep, or is pumped too hard, can draw the salt water up.

items.p: Who should decide how much groundwater the farms of a village may pump?

views.who: A farmer who needs water for her fields
views.says: The farmers should decide. We know our land, and our crops need water every season.

views.who: A woman who draws water from the village well
views.says: Everyone who uses the water should decide, because when farms pump too much, the village well runs dry.
Someone should measure how fast the rain refills the ground. The pumping limit should follow that number.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason: groundwater is shared under many fields, so one farm's pumping affects the others. Another: a measured limit stops arguments, but people who use the water should help to set it.
items.why: A strong answer sees that groundwater is shared, and links the limit to how fast rain refills it. It gives the other views a fair hearing.

items.p: Draw the journey of one drop of fresh water from the sea back to the sea. Mark where the salt stays.
items.a: The drop rises from the sea as vapour and the salt stays in the sea. It forms a cloud, falls as rain or snow, runs down a river or soaks into the ground, and flows back to the sea, where it meets salt again.
items.why: A strong drawing shows evaporation leaving the salt in the sea, and the river carrying fresh water back to where it picks up salt.
items.art: A blank sheet with a sea at the bottom, a mountain on one side, and space for clouds, a river and arrows.

items.p: In Freeze the Sea, the taster did not know which drop was which. Say what could go wrong if they knew.
items.a: A taster who knew which drop was the ice might expect it to taste fresh, and taste it that way. Knowing could change what they report. Not knowing keeps the result honest.
items.why: A strong answer says that expecting a result can change what a person tastes or sees, and that a blind test removes this.

items.p: Body liquids hold 9 grams of salt in a litre. Sea water holds 35. About how many times saltier is the sea?
items.why: 35 divided by 9 is about 3.9, so the sea is about 4 times as salty as the liquids in the body.

items.p: Sea water holds 35 grams of salt in a litre. Suppose urine holds at most 20. How much urine carries that salt?
items.why: 35 grams divided by 20 grams in each litre is 1.75 litres. The person drank 1 litre, so the body loses three quarters of a litre more than it took in.

items.p: If the Earth's water were 2 litres in all, about how many millilitres would be fresh?
items.why: About 25 parts in 1,000 are fresh. 2 litres is 2,000 millilitres. 25 times 2 is 50 millilitres.

items.p: If all the floating ice at the North Pole melted, the sea would rise by metres.
items.why: False. The ice at the North Pole is sea ice that already floats. It pushes aside its own weight of water, so melting it changes the sea level very little. This matches tumbler A.

items.p: Which melting ice would add the most water to the sea?
opts: The ice sheets on Greenland and Antarctica
The sea ice around the North Pole
Ice cubes floating in a tumbler
An iceberg that is already floating
items.why: These ice sheets sit on land, like the ice in the strainer. Their melt water is new water for the sea. The others already float.

items.p: Put these in order, from the saltiest to the least salty:
items.why: The Dead Sea holds about 340 grams in a litre and the Arabian Sea about 36. Chilika in the monsoon is a few grams, and rain has almost none.

items.p: A coastal town's wells turned salty after years of heavy pumping. Explain how this happens and one way to stop it.
items.a: Fresh groundwater floats on sea water and holds it back from the land. When too much fresh water is pumped out, the sea water moves inland under the ground and reaches the wells. The town can pump less, catch rain, and let the rain refill the ground.
items.why: A strong answer says that fresh water floats on salt water, and that taking out too much lets the salt water move in. It gives a fix that lets rain refill the ground.

items.p: Should a river be pumped for a city if the fish and fishers at the river's mouth lose out?

views.says: Millions of people need water to drink. A river is the cheapest place to get it.

views.who: A fisher at the river mouth
views.says: When too much river water is taken, the mouth turns salty. The fish who breed there are gone, and so is my work.
The river should be shared. Each of us should take only what the river can refill.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason: a river that no longer reaches the sea changes the estuary, and the fish breed where fresh and salt water meet. Another: millions of people's drinking water matters first, and the plan can still leave some flow for the river.
items.why: A strong answer sees that taking from a river affects the estuary at its end. It does not treat the engineer, fisher or farmer as wrong, because each has a real need.

items.p: Freezing sea water gives ice that is not perfectly fresh. What is the best explanation?
opts: Pockets of salty liquid are trapped between the ice crystals
Ice makes a little new salt
The freezer adds salt to the ice
The water did not freeze at all
items.why: Ice crystals push most salt out, but salty liquid gets trapped in small pockets between them. That is why old sea ice, where the pockets have drained, is nearly fresh.

items.p: Many people say that a deeper well gives fresher water. Plan a test of this in a village near the sea.
items.a: Choose wells of different depths in the same village. Take a sample from each in the same way and at the same time of year. Tasting the water is not safe, so test them for salt with a safe method such as a grown-up's meter or the village health office. Compare depth with saltiness for all the wells.
items.why: A strong answer compares several wells of different depths, keeps everything else the same, and measures saltiness safely, not by drinking.

items.p: Match each change to what happens to the salt.
pairs: The salt stays in the sea
Most salt stays in the liquid
Salts build up year after year
It picks up a little salt from the rock
items.why: Salt is left behind when water leaves as vapour or ice. A lake with no outlet loses water only by evaporation, and rain on rock picks up dissolved salts.

items.p: Draw two tumblers after Ice on Land, Ice on Sea. Show each water line, and label the one that rose.
items.a: Two tumblers with a band marked on each. In tumbler A the water is level with the band. In tumbler B the water is above the band, and the label says it rose.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the band and the water line in both tumblers, with only the tumbler that had ice above the water showing a rise.
items.art: Two blank tumbler outlines with a dotted line marking the start water line on each.

items.p: Which statement about the three forms of water is true?
opts: Most of Earth's water is liquid
Most of Earth's water is ice
Most of Earth's water is vapour
Most of Earth's water is cloud
items.why: About 98 of every 100 parts of Earth's water are liquid, in the sea and under the ground. Nearly 2 parts are ice, and vapour is only about 1 part in 100,000.

items.p: Most of the fresh water that people take from rivers, lakes and the ground goes to homes.
items.why: False. Worldwide, about 7 in 10 litres go to farms, about 2 to industry, and about 1 to homes.

quiz.p: About how many grams of salt does one litre of sea water hold?
quiz.why: A litre of sea water holds about 35 grams of dissolved salts, which is about 6 level teaspoons. Fresh water holds under 1 gram.

quiz.p: In One Litre Earth, what stands for all the fresh lakes and rivers in the world?
quiz.why: All the fresh lakes and rivers together are less than one tenth of one part in 1,000. That is about one drop in a litre.

quiz.p: A cloud is made of what?
opts: Tiny drops of water or tiny bits of ice
quiz.why: Water vapour is invisible. A cloud forms when vapour condenses into tiny drops, or freezes into tiny bits of ice, which are big enough to see.

quiz.p: Which change takes the salt out of sea water?
quiz.why: Only the water particles fly into the air. The salt stays behind. Stirring and a cloth do not separate dissolved salt.

quiz.p: Why does a person who drinks sea water become thirstier?
opts: The kidneys need extra water to remove the salt
The body keeps the salt and loses nothing
Sea water has no water in it
quiz.why: The kidneys can make urine only a little more than half as salty as sea water. So they must use extra body water to carry the salt out.

quiz.p: Why does fresh water float on sea water?
opts: A litre of it has less mass
quiz.why: A litre of fresh water has a mass of about 1,000 grams and a litre of sea water about 1,025 grams. The lighter water floats.

quiz.p: Which melting ice raises the sea?
opts: Ice on land, such as on Greenland
Ice floating at the North Pole
Ice cubes floating in a tumbler
quiz.why: Ice on land adds new water to the sea. Floating ice already pushes aside its own weight of water, so it changes the level very little.

quiz.p: Why does a fair test change only one thing at a time?
opts: So that we know what caused the difference
So there is less to wash up
quiz.why: If two things change, we cannot tell which one caused the result. In Freeze the Sea, only the salt differed between the bowls.

quiz.p: What takes the largest share of the fresh water that people use, worldwide?
quiz.why: About 7 of every 10 litres go to farms, because growing plants take up a great deal of water. Homes use about 1 in 10.

quiz.p: Which holds more fresh water: all the lakes and rivers, or the groundwater?
opts: Lakes and rivers, about 100 times more
quiz.why: In One Litre Earth, groundwater is about 1 and a half teaspoons, and all the lakes and rivers are about one drop. Most liquid fresh water is under the ground.

quiz.p: An albatross drinks sea water and stays healthy. How?
opts: Salt glands above her eyes remove the salt
She drinks only a very little
Her kidneys are the same as ours
The salt falls out of her feathers
quiz.why: The glands take salt out of her blood and make a very salty liquid, which drips from her beak. Humans have no such glands.

opts: Water where a river meets the sea
Water from a village well in the hills
quiz.why: Brackish water is saltier than fresh water but less salty than the sea. Rivers and the sea mix where a river reaches the coast.

applications: A hospital drip bag holds normal saline, which has 9 grams of salt in a litre. That is the same saltiness as blood, so the cells do not swell or shrink.
People make pickles and dry fish with a lot of salt. The salt pulls water out of the food and out of germs, so the food keeps for months.
A sea-water plant such as the one at Minjur near Chennai makes drinking water from the sea. It pushes sea water through very fine sheets at high pressure, which hold back the salt.
Salt pans at Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu and in Gujarat let the Sun evaporate sea water. The salt is left in the pan. Gujarat makes most of India's salt this way.
Oral rehydration solution, which is sold in small packets in India, mixes the right amounts of salt and sugar in water. It helps a body that has lost water in a stomach illness to take water in.
Himalayan glaciers feed the Ganga, the Indus and the Brahmaputra in summer. Cities and farms along these rivers plan their water around the snow and ice.
Villages on coral islands such as those of Lakshadweep keep wells shallow and pump gently, so that the thin layer of rain water does not mix with the sea water under it.

open_questions.q: How much water is locked deep inside the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: A speck of a deep mineral inside one Brazilian diamond held water. One speck is not enough to say how much water is in all the deep rock, which nobody can drill into.

open_questions.q: How fast will the ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica melt, and how high will the sea rise?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on how the ice flows and breaks, and on how much warmer Earth becomes. Different computer models give different answers.

open_questions.q: How much groundwater is left under India and under the world?
open_questions.why_open: The water is hidden underground. Satellites show that it is falling in some places, but measuring the amount that is left is very hard.

open_questions.q: Where did Earth's water come from?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think much of it came with the rock that formed Earth. Others think a large share arrived later on asteroids and comets. Nobody yet knows how much each gave.

open_questions.q: Can taking salt out of sea water ever be cheap and gentle enough for everyone?
open_questions.why_open: It needs a great deal of energy, and it leaves very salty waste. Engineers are looking for ways to use less energy and to put the waste to use.

ask_kids: Where does the water in our tap fall as rain? Which sea does it flow to?
At a meal, what is salty in our food? Where did that salt once come from?
If you were on a boat with no fresh water, what would you do?
Which people near us use the most water? What do they use it for?
Why can a fish live in the sea, when a person cannot drink it?
When you see an ice cube float in a drink, what do you notice about how much is above the water?
What water near us is fresh, and what is salty or in between?
If it did not rain for a year, where would our water come from?

jokes.j: What did the sea say to the beach?
What do you call a lake with no way out?
Why did the lagoon feel confused?
jokes.a: It could not decide between the river and the sea.

jokes.j: Why is a salt pan a good worker?
jokes.a: The Sun does the work, and the pan keeps the salt.

jokes.j: Why did the albatross carry no handkerchief?
jokes.a: Her salt gland drips from her beak.

jokes.j: Why was the cloud never salty?

maths.problem: In One Litre Earth, 25 millilitres of the 1,000 are fresh. What fraction of the bottle is fresh, in its simplest form? What percentage is that?
maths.answer: One fortieth of the bottle, which is 2 and a half out of every 100.
maths.explain: 25 out of 1,000 is 25 over 1,000. Divide the top and the bottom by 25 to get 1 over 40. As a percentage, 25 divided by 1,000 is 0.025, which is 2.5 in every 100.
maths.context: In One Litre Earth, a one-litre bottle stands for all of Earth's water. Five teaspoons, or 25 millilitres, stand for the fresh water.
maths.why_maths: A fraction in its simplest form shows at a glance how small a share is. One in 40 is easier to picture than 25 in 1,000.

maths.problem: A tumbler holds about 13 tablespoons. After freezing, the melted ice measured 6 tablespoons and the liquid measured 5. How much water was lost, and what fraction froze?
maths.answer: 2 tablespoons were lost. A little under half froze, which is 6 out of 13.
maths.explain: 6 plus 5 is 11. The tumbler held 13, so 13 minus 11 is 2 tablespoons lost in rinsing and straining. The ice was 6 out of 13, which is a little less than half, because half of 13 is 6 and a half.
maths.context: In Freeze the Sea, you measure the melted ice and the leftover liquid in tablespoons. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: Adding the parts and comparing them with the start shows how much water was lost, and how much of the water froze.

maths.problem: Sea water holds 35 grams of salt in a litre. A bucket holds 8 litres of sea water, and the Sun dries it all. How many grams of salt are left, and about how many level teaspoons is that if one holds 6 grams?
maths.explain: 8 times 35 is 280 grams. 280 divided by 6 is about 46.7, so about 47 teaspoons. Evaporation took the water and left every gram of salt.
maths.context: Evaporation takes water out of sea water and leaves the salt. Salt pans such as those at Thoothukudi work this way.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a rate by an amount gives the total salt, and dividing by a teaspoon's mass turns grams into a kitchen measure.

maths.problem: SEA holds about 30 grams of salt in a litre. A lagoon mix is 3 parts of sea water and 7 parts of plain water. How salty is it? Is it saltier or less salty than the liquids in your body, which hold 9 grams?
maths.answer: 9 grams in a litre. It is about as salty as the liquids in your body.
maths.explain: 3 parts out of 10 is three tenths. Three tenths of 30 is 9. The body's liquids also hold about 9 grams in a litre, so the mix is about the same.
maths.context: In Mix a Lagoon, you mix sea-strength water with plain water in different amounts, and work out how salty each mix is.
maths.why_maths: A mix of two parts is a fraction of the stronger water, so a ratio tells you the saltiness of the mix without testing it.

maths.problem: Suppose urine can hold at most 20 grams of salt in a litre. How many litres of urine does a person need to carry out the 35 grams of salt in 1 litre of sea water? How much more water than the person drank is lost?
maths.answer: 1.75 litres of urine, so 0.75 litres more than the person drank.
maths.explain: 35 divided by 20 is 1.75. The person drank 1 litre, so the body loses 1.75 minus 1, which is 0.75 litres more than it took in.
maths.context: A person who drinks sea water must get rid of the salt through the kidneys. The 20 grams is a made-up round number.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the salt by what each litre of urine can carry shows why sea water leaves a person with less water, not more.

maths.problem: A roof of 80 square metres gets 1,200 millimetres of rain in a year. How many litres fall on it? A tank catches 7 tenths of that. How many litres is that?
maths.answer: 96,000 litres fall. The tank catches 67,200 litres.
maths.explain: One millimetre on one square metre is one litre. 80 times 1,200 is 96,000 litres. Seven tenths of 96,000 is 9,600 times 7, which is 67,200 litres.
maths.context: In The Roof and the Tap, you work out how many litres of rain fall on your own roof. These are made-up numbers.
maths.why_maths: Area times depth gives volume. The sum turns a weather report in millimetres into litres a family can use.

maths.problem: In One Litre Earth, the ice is 17 millilitres. About 9 tenths of the world's ice is on Antarctica. How many millilitres of the ice is that? About how many teaspoons?
maths.answer: About 15 millilitres, which is about 3 teaspoons.
maths.explain: Nine tenths of 17 is 15.3 millilitres. A teaspoon holds 5 millilitres, and 15.3 divided by 5 is about 3. So the ice of Antarctica is about 3 of the 5 teaspoons of fresh water.
maths.context: In One Litre Earth, the ice is a heap of about 3 and a half teaspoons. Most of that ice lies on Antarctica.
maths.why_maths: Finding a fraction of a fraction of the whole shows that one ice sheet holds most of the fresh water on Earth.

how_we_found_out.context: This is the true story of how people found out that ice made from sea water leaves the salt behind. You test the same thing in Freeze the Sea.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1770s, British explorers wanted to know if ships could sail to the North Pole across open sea. Some thinkers said yes. Some thinkers doubted that sea water could freeze hard, because it is salty. Any ice that explorers met at sea, they said, must have come from rivers and the land. Edward Nairne, a London maker of scientific instruments, tested the idea. In 1776 he set sea water out in the winter cold. It froze, though only a little below the cold that freezes pond water. He then melted the ice, and the water had no taste of salt. The salt had stayed in the liquid that was left. So sea water does freeze, and freezing takes most of the salt out. Later explorers found that the polar sea was covered with ice that the sea itself had made.
how_we_found_out.who: Edward Nairne, a maker of scientific instruments in London, who tested whether the ice of sea water is fresh
how_we_found_out.when: Nairne froze sea water in 1776, in the years when British explorers were sailing north.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That sea water cannot freeze hard, so ice found at sea must have come from rivers or from the land. Nairne froze sea water and melted the ice. It was nearly fresh, so the sea can freeze and the ice leaves most of the salt behind.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in eighteenth-century clothes on a snowy London rooftop at night, bending over shallow dishes of water with a thermometer in his hand.

roots.context: In this unit you froze salty water and found that the ice left most of the salt behind. Here we ask what that tells us about fresh water, the sea and ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In One Litre Earth, all the fresh lakes and rivers of the world fill less than one drop. Even so, rivers have kept running for millions of years. The Sun lifts fresh water out of the sea and leaves the salt behind. Then rain brings the water back. So a place can keep using water for ever only if it takes no more than the rain refills.
deep_truth.habit: We call Earth a water planet, so it seems that water can never run short. That counts the sea, which people cannot drink. The water that people can actually use is only a small amount. It is what the Sun lifts out of the sea and the rain brings back.
deep_truth.evidence: In One Litre Earth, the sea and the ice fill almost the whole bottle. All the lakes and rivers together are only one drop. In Freeze the Sea, ice leaves its salt behind, and evaporation does the same over the sea.

three.who_am_i: More than half of your body is water, and that water holds about 9 grams of salt in a litre. Your body keeps that amount steady every hour, with every drink and every visit to the toilet.
three.what_is_life: Every living cell is a small bag of slightly salty water. An albatross, a mangrove and a child each have their own way of keeping that water at the right saltiness.
three.what_is_this_world: The sea, the clouds, the glaciers and the rivers hold the same water at different times. The Sun and the cold keep taking water out of the sea, and the rivers keep taking it back.

roots.thread: A drop of water in the Bay of Bengal carries salt. The Sun lifts the water into the air and the salt stays in the sea. The drop falls as snow on a Himalayan glacier and melts into the Ganga. It may pass through a well, a tumbler and a child. Then it flows back to the bay and mixes with salt again. The same water passes through the sea, a cloud, a glacier, a river and a child, one after another.

teachings.teaching: The rivers in the east flow east and the rivers in the west flow west. They rise from the sea and go back to the sea, and they become the sea. Once there, they do not know 'I am this river' or 'I am that river'.
teachings.link: The verse says that rivers come from the sea and return to it. This unit's science agrees: rain rises from the sea by evaporation, and rivers carry it back. science.text: Matter is not made or destroyed when water changes form. The water that freezes, melts, evaporates and condenses is the same water.
Nearly all the water in rivers, lakes, glaciers and groundwater fell as rain or snow, and most of that vapour rose from the sea.
Deep rock inside the Earth may hold as much water as all the oceans, locked inside minerals. Nobody yet knows how much.

other_view.who: A doctor who treats people with dehydration
other_view.view: For a living body, fresh water and sea water are truly different, because one keeps a person alive and the other dries them out. Calling them the same water ignores the difference that matters to a thirsty person. So, on this view, what water does to a living body is part of what water is.

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. None of them has been tried at home yet, so treat the expected results as likely, not certain. Freeze the Sea (core) needs a freezer and two to four hours. Salt water freezes a little later than plain water, and its ice is soft. If the bowl freezes solid before you look, the step says how to thaw it over a strainer. The melted ice usually still tastes a little salty, which is part of the lesson. The Potato Test (core) needs one raw potato and a grown-up to cut it. The sticks must be thin, about as thick as a pencil, or one hour is too short to see a change. The length changes are small, so the bend test is the clearer result. Ice on Land, Ice on Sea needs two straight-sided tumblers, a tea strainer wide enough to rest on the rim, and an hour of waiting. The tumbler with floating ice should stay within a millimetre or two of its band. The other should rise by about 10 to 20 millimetres. If the strainer touches the water, pour a little water out and mark the line again. One Litre Earth (core) needs only a bottle, a teaspoon and a katori. The amounts are rounded, so a little more or less is fine. One Bottle, Three Forms (core) takes three days. Use a plastic cup, never glass, in the freezer. The ice may rise as a small bump, and the open cup may lose only one to three millimetres of water in a day. The Island Well works only if the clear water is poured very slowly over a spoon. If the whole jar turns pale blue, empty it and try again more slowly. A straw sample is a few drops, so keep the thumb tight on the top of the straw. Mix a Lagoon needs one teaspoon of salt, and a taster can tell PLAIN from MONSOON only with care. Pin the Fresh Water needs a world map or an atlas. The Roof and the Tap needs the area of a roof and the yearly rain of your town. A child must not climb on any roof. The rain figures in the notes are rounded, so look up your own town if you can. Fresher Ice needs a freezer and takes most of a day. A second freezing leaves less water, so the sample is small. The blind taste is the only measure, so a very small difference may not be noticed, and that is a fair result. A Water Plan for a Small Island needs only paper and a calculator, and its numbers are made up. Fresh, Salty or In Between needs scissors and 27 small cards. Sea to Glass needs a die, a button for each player, a grain of rice for each player and about 12 beans. Nothing needs a garden or an animal. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026: the shares of Earth's water (USGS), the Antarctic ice figures, the paper citations, Nairne's 1776 paper and its title, the glacier lengths, the Minjur and Kavaratti plants, the Indian drinking-water standard and the groundwater shares. Softened: the sea ice salt share, the Siachen length, the urine salt limit (now a made-up figure in the maths), the iceberg and hand-pump lines, the age of the Tirukkural, and the Agatti size. Removed: Daines Barrington as the person who argued the idea, the Bay of Bengal salt figure, and two boat-landing names. The readings of the Tirukkural verse and the Upanishad verse are paraphrases.
